blocks.text:
### How to use this guide

- **Who this is for.** A Java full stack developer who must explain, and diagnose, what the operating system does beneath a running service: process and thread management, memory, files, I/O, containers and synchronisation.
- **Every chapter follows the same steps:** (1) the concept and the problem it solves, (2) the mechanism, shown with diagrams, (3) a worked trace or calculation, (4) a hands-on experiment with real commands, C or Java code, (5) **real-world incidents**, each presented as symptoms, diagnosis, root cause, fix and prevention, and (6) the questions interviewers ask, with answers.
- **How to study.** Read each diagram before the prose and narrate it aloud. Reproduce every experiment on a Linux machine or virtual machine (never on a production host). Treat each incident as an exercise: cover the diagnosis, decide which command to run first, then compare with the text.
- **Running the code.** Save a Java listing as `Main.java` and run `java Main.java`; compile C with `gcc -O0 -o demo` `demo.c`. Terminal sessions begin with `$`. Output shown was produced on the build machine unless labelled typical.
- **Scope.** The focus is Linux, the platform on which most Java services run, together with the JVM and container behaviour that interacts with it. Windows and macOS are mentioned only where the difference matters.

sections.title: How to Approach a System Design Interview

blocks.text:
A system design problem is deliberately under-specified: "design a news feed" or "design a ticket-booking service" admits thousands of valid answers and no single correct one. The evaluation therefore concentrates on the process by which a candidate narrows the problem, quantifies it, selects components and defends trade-offs. A candidate who begins drawing boxes within the first minute usually builds a design for a problem that was never posed. A candidate who follows a fixed framework spends the available time on the decisions that matter and leaves a written trail that the interviewer can steer.

This chapter defines a seven-step framework, assigns a time budget to each step for a 45-minute session, separates functional from non-functional requirements, lists the mistakes that cost the most points, and applies the framework to a small worked example. The case-study chapters that follow in later Parts use the same section order, so the framework also serves as a reading guide.

### The seven-step framework

The framework consists of seven steps. Each step produces a concrete artefact that is written on the board, which keeps the discussion anchored and allows the interviewer to correct a wrong assumption early, when the correction is cheap.

blocks.text:
#### Step 1: clarify requirements

Clarification converts a vague prompt into a scoped problem. The questions fall into five groups:

- **Users and use cases.** Who uses the system (consumers, internal staff, other services), and which three or four features are essential? The candidate proposes a minimal feature set and asks for confirmation instead of enumerating every conceivable feature.
- **Scale.** Daily active users, peak concurrency, growth horizon, read-to-write ratio, geographic distribution.
- **Quality attributes.** Latency expectations, availability target, consistency requirements, durability expectations, data retention.
- **Constraints.** Existing technology, team size, regulatory requirements, budget, build versus buy.
- **Out of scope.** Explicitly stated exclusions such as billing, administration consoles, or machine-learning ranking, so that the interviewer can confirm that the exclusion is acceptable.

Requirements are classified into two kinds. A **functional requirement** states what the system does ("a user can post a message; followers see it in a feed"). A **non-functional requirement** (also called a quality attribute) states how well the system does it ("a feed loads in under 200 ms at the 99th percentile; the service is available 99.95 percent of the time"). Functional requirements determine which components exist; non-functional requirements determine how those components are arranged, replicated and scaled.

blocks.alt: Non-functional requirement Design lever it drives | Latency target | cache, CDN, async work, fewer hops | p99 under 200 ms | Throughput | horizontal scale, partitioning, batching | peak 35 K reads/s | Availability | redundancy, failover, load shedding | 99.95 percent | Consistency | leader reads, quorum, session routing | read-your-writes | Durability | replication, WAL, backups | no acknowledged write lost | Cost | tiered storage, TTLs, compression | fixed monthly budget

blocks.text:
A non-functional requirement without a number cannot drive a decision. "Fast" is not a requirement; "p99 read latency below 200 ms" is. When the interviewer does not supply a number, the candidate proposes one, labels it as an assumption and continues.

#### Step 2: estimate

Back-of-the-envelope estimation (the next chapter treats the technique in detail) establishes the order of magnitude of the load. The purpose is not accuracy but the selection of a design regime: 100 requests per second fit on one server; 100 000 per second do not. Three results are almost always needed: peak requests per second, total storage over the retention period, and peak network bandwidth. A fourth, working-set memory, decides whether a cache is useful.

#### Step 3: API design

The API fixes the contract between clients and the system. For each core use case the candidate writes one operation with its method and path (or RPC name), parameters, response, and error behaviour. Four properties are discussed whenever they are relevant: **pagination** for list endpoints (cursor-based pagination is preferred for large or changing collections, because offset pagination degrades and returns duplicates under concurrent writes); **idempotency** for operations with side effects (a client-supplied idempotency key makes retries safe); **authentication and** **authorisation** (stated, not designed in detail unless the prompt targets it); and **versioning**.

#### Step 4: data model

The data model is derived from the access patterns, not from the entities alone. For each query that the API implies, the candidate states which key is used to find the data, how the data is partitioned across nodes, and which index supports the query. The choice between a relational store and a NoSQL store follows from those patterns and from the consistency requirements, as covered in the databases material; here the decision is justified in one sentence per store.

#### Step 5: high-level design

The high-level design is a block diagram plus two or three numbered request flows (for instance, the write path and the read path). Components are added only when a requirement or a number justifies them: a cache appears because a read-to-write ratio of 100 to 1 was established in step 2, a queue appears because a write must be acknowledged before slow processing finishes. Every arrow in the diagram is labelled with the protocol or the data it carries.

#### Step 6: deep dive

The interviewer typically selects one or two components for depth, or accepts the candidate's proposal. A deep dive follows a fixed pattern: state the problem and its numbers, list two or three alternatives, compare them in a table against the relevant criteria, select one, and state the assumption that drives the choice together with the condition under which the choice would be reversed. The second and third parts of this book apply the pattern to more than twenty systems.

#### Step 7: wrap-up

The wrap-up addresses what the design does not yet cover: single points of failure, behaviour under overload, monitoring (which metrics and alerts would show the design failing), security, and the next two extensions. A candidate who names the weakest part of the own design before the interviewer does is evaluated more favourably than one who presents the design as flawless.

### Time management for a 45-minute interview

blocks.alt: Phase Clarify Estimate API Data High-level design Deep dive Wrap-up | Output scope list numbers endpoints tables diagram + flows 2-3 hard parts risks | 0 5 10 15 20 30 40 45

blocks.text:
The allocation above is a guideline, not a rule. Two adjustments are common. When the prompt is a familiar one (a URL shortener), steps 1 to 4 compress to 12 to 15 minutes, which leaves more time for the deep dive. When the interviewer interrupts with questions, the time belongs to the interviewer's agenda, and the candidate resumes the framework at the step that was interrupted. In a 60-minute session the extra 15 minutes belong to the deep dive and the wrap-up.

A short checkpoint at the end of each step keeps the session on schedule: "The scope is: post, follow, feed. Scale is 100 million daily users. Shall the estimation proceed?" The checkpoint costs ten seconds and prevents a long divergence.

### Worked example: a page-view counter service

The example is deliberately small so that every step fits in a few lines. The prompt is: "Design a service that counts page views for a website and shows the count on each page."

#### Step 1: clarification (answers assumed)

- Functional: record a view of a page; return the view count of a page; counts need not be exact to the last view.
- Non-functional: record path acknowledged in under 50 ms at p99; read path under 100 ms at p99; availability 99.95 percent; counts may lag real time by up to 5 seconds (eventual consistency is acceptable); no view is lost once acknowledged.
- Scale (assumed): 1 billion page views per day, 50 million distinct pages, 5 years of retention of daily totals.
- Out of scope: unique-visitor counting, bot filtering, per-user analytics, dashboards.

#### Step 2: estimation

rows: 1 read per view (page render shows the count)
same as writes, about 35 K/s at peak
page id (8 B) + timestamp (8 B) + overhead (about 84 B)
about 0.8 GB: fits in memory of one node
blocks.caption: Estimates for the counter service (all inputs assumed).

blocks.text:
The two numbers that shape the design are 35 K writes per second at peak, which is more than a single relational row-update path should absorb for hot pages, and the 0.8 GB counter state, which is small enough to cache entirely.

#### Step 3: API

**Counter API**

blocks.code:
POST /v1/views
     body: {"pageId": "p-123"}
     -> 202 Accepted
GET  /v1/pages/{pageId}/views
     -> 200 {"pageId": "p-123", "views": 91823}
GET  /v1/pages/{pageId}/views?bucket=day&from=2026-10-01&to=2026-10-07
     -> 200 [{"day": "2026-10-01", "views": 120}, {"day": "2026-10-02", "views": 133}]

blocks.text:
The write returns 202 (accepted for processing) rather than 200, which states honestly that the count is updated asynchronously. No idempotency key is required because the semantics are "at least one view recorded"; if exactly-once counting were required, the request would carry an event identifier and the aggregator would deduplicate.

#### Step 4: data model

blocks.title: Counter tables

blocks.text:
The partitioning key is the page identifier, so that all updates of one page reach one partition and the read for a page touches one partition.

#### Steps 5 and 6: high-level design and deep dive

blocks.text: The deep dive concerns one problem: 35 K increments per second must not become 35 K row updates per second, because a popular page would then serialise on a single row. Three alternatives are compared:

rows: Row-lock contention on hot pages; write latency tied to the database
In-memory counter per API node, periodic flush
Each node sums locally and flushes every second
Very cheap; reduces writes by the batch factor
A node crash loses up to one second of counts (violates the no-loss requirement)
Events are appended durably, then summed per page per window
Durable once acknowledged; batch factor reduces database writes; absorbs spikes
One more component; counts lag by the window (1 to 5 s)
blocks.caption: Alternatives for the write path.

blocks.text:
The third alternative is selected because the requirement "no acknowledged view is lost" excludes the second, and the tolerance of a few seconds of lag permits the third. The assumption that drives the decision is the lag tolerance; if exact real-time counts were required, the design would return to synchronous updates with sharded counters (one logical counter split across several rows that are summed on read).

#### Step 7: wrap-up

- Single points of failure: the queue is replicated (three replicas, assumed); aggregator workers are stateless and restart from the last committed offset.
- Overload: the API applies admission control and returns 429 when the queue append latency exceeds a threshold (see the chapter on availability and reliability in this Part).
- Monitoring: consumer lag (seconds behind), queue append p99, aggregator batch size, cache hit ratio, database write rate.
- Extensions: unique visitors via a probabilistic structure (HyperLogLog), per-region counts, bot filtering upstream.

### Mistakes that cost the most points

rows: Drawing the architecture before stating requirements
Spend the first five minutes on scope; write the list on the board
Numbers without arithmetic, or arithmetic without assumptions
Show each multiplication and label every input as an assumption
Naming technologies instead of properties ("use Kafka")
State the property needed (durable, ordered, replayable log), then name a technology that provides it
Adding components that no requirement justifies
Tie every component to a number or a requirement
A single design with no alternatives
For each major decision, name at least one alternative and the reason for rejecting it
For every stateful component, state what happens when it fails or lags
Treating the interviewer as an examiner instead of a collaborator
Offer checkpoints; adopt hints; follow the interviewer's chosen deep dive
Over-engineering for planet scale when the numbers are modest
Let the estimate choose the regime: one database with a replica is correct for 200 requests per second
State the decision under consideration, for example "choosing between cache-aside and write-through"
blocks.caption: Frequent mistakes and corrections.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How is a system design interview evaluated? Typical rubrics weigh four areas: problem exploration (requirements, scope, assumptions), technical depth (data model, component choices, correctness of the reasoning), trade-off analysis (alternatives and the conditions under which each wins), and communication (structure, use of numbers, response to hints). Correct component names carry little weight on their own; a justified decision with a stated assumption carries much more.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. Why are requirements clarified before any design?

The same prompt yields different designs for 1 000 and for 100 million users, and for strong versus eventual consistency. Clarification fixes those parameters, prevents the design of a system that was not requested, and demonstrates the engineering habit of scoping before building.

#### 2. How is a non-functional requirement turned into a design decision?

By attaching a number and then mapping the number to a lever: a p99 latency target of 200 ms limits the number of sequential network hops and suggests caching; an availability target of 99.95 percent (about 4.4 hours of downtime per year) requires redundancy across failure domains; a durability requirement excludes designs that acknowledge a write before it is replicated.

#### 3. What is to be done when the interviewer provides no numbers?

Propose round, defensible assumptions, state them aloud, and ask whether they are acceptable. For example: "I assume 100 million daily active users, 10 reads and 0.1 writes per user per day." The estimate remains valid because every later number derives from the stated assumptions and can be recomputed if the interviewer changes one.

#### 4. How does a candidate choose which component to deep-dive?

The deep dive targets the component whose failure or scaling limit would invalidate the design: the hottest data path, the component with the weakest consistency story, or the one the estimate shows to be at the edge of a single node. The interviewer's interest overrides the candidate's choice.

#### 5. What is the difference between a design that "works" and one that is "good"?

A working design satisfies the functional requirements at the stated scale. A good design also states which requirement each component serves, identifies its own bottlenecks and failure modes, gives alternatives with reasons for rejection, and remains simple enough that the stated team could operate it.

#### 6. How is time recovered when the discussion runs long?

By summarising the current step in one sentence, recording any open question on the board as a follow-up item, and moving to the next step. Skipping the wrap-up is the most common and most damaging way to run out of time; it is protected by reserving the last five minutes.

#### 7. Is it acceptable to name a specific product?

Yes, provided the property that motivates the choice is stated and an alternative is acknowledged. "A partitioned, replicated log such as Kafka, because the aggregator needs durable, replayable ordered input; a managed queue would also work if replay is not required" is a complete statement.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- The seven steps are: clarify, estimate, API, data model, high-level design, deep dive, wrap-up; each produces a visible artefact.
- Functional requirements decide which components exist; numeric non-functional requirements decide how they are arranged and scaled.
- Every number is labelled as an assumption and shown with its arithmetic; every component is tied to a requirement or a number.
- A deep dive compares alternatives in a table, selects one, and states the assumption that drives the choice.
- A 45-minute budget is 5, 5, 5, 5, 10, 10 and 5 minutes; the wrap-up is protected.
- A design that names its own weaknesses is evaluated above one that claims none.

Capacity estimation answers one question before any component is drawn: which regime does the system belong to? A service that peaks at 200 requests per second and stores 50 GB is served by one application server, one primary database and one replica. A service that peaks at 400 000 requests per second and stores 600 TB requires partitioning, caching tiers and a content delivery network. The architecture differs in kind, not only in degree, and the estimate selects between the two.

The estimate is intentionally coarse. A result within a factor of two to three of reality is sufficient, because the design decisions that follow depend on orders of magnitude. The discipline consists of three habits: state every input as an assumption, show every multiplication, and round aggressively to keep the arithmetic mental.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Numbers to memorise

Storage and traffic estimates rely on a small set of constants.

#### Latency numbers

The relative cost of operations determines where a design places data. The following figures are the classical list attributed to Jeff Dean and reproduced by Peter Norvig (norvig.com/21-days.html, "Approximate timing for various operations on a typical PC"). They date from about 2009 and describe orders of magnitude: absolute values have improved (solid-state storage and faster networks), but the ratios between memory, storage and network remain instructive.

blocks.text: Two further values appear in most versions of the list that circulate among engineers (for example the interactive tables derived from Dean's 2009 talk); they are quoted here as orders of magnitude and not verified for current hardware: a round trip within one data center is about 0.5 ms, and a random 4 KB read from a solid-state drive is about 0.1 to 0.15 ms. Cloud network round trips between availability zones of one region are commonly in the range of one to a few milliseconds; the exact value must be measured on the platform in use.

blocks.text:
Four conclusions follow from the table:

- Memory is roughly three orders of magnitude faster than a network round trip within a data center, and five orders faster than a cross-continent one. Caching saves a network trip, not only a disk access.
- Sequential access beats random access by a large factor on rotating disks (reading 1 MB sequentially costs 20 ms; each seek costs 8 ms). Log-structured and append-only designs exploit this.
- Compressing data before it crosses a slow link is usually profitable, because computation is far cheaper than transmission.
- Round trips accumulate: a request that performs 20 sequential calls inside one data center spends about 10 ms in the network alone.

#### The estimation formulas

`daily read bytes x hot fraction (often 20 percent by the 80/20` `rule; an upper bound, because repeated reads of the same object` `count once in the working set)`

blocks.caption: Core formulas.

blocks.text:
The peak factor deserves attention. Traffic is not uniform: a daily cycle typically yields a peak-hour rate two to three times the daily average, and events (a sale, a live match) produce short bursts of ten times or more. The system is sized for the peak plus headroom, not for the average.

The read-to-write ratio is the second parameter that shapes a design. Ratios of 100 to 1 and above (a URL shortener, a content site) favour caching and replicas; ratios near 1 to 1 or below (metrics ingestion, logging) favour append-optimised, partitioned storage.

Per-server capacity is itself an assumption that must be measured for the real application. Planning values often quoted as orders of magnitude, not guarantees: a stateless application server performing little work per request handles hundreds to a few thousand requests per second per core-pair, an in-memory key-value store handles on the order of 100 000 simple operations per second per instance, and a single relational database node handles thousands to tens of thousands of simple queries per second depending on the query and the hardware. These values guide the first sketch and are replaced by measurements (see load testing in a later chapter).

### Worked example

Three systems of very different shape are estimated with the same formulas. Every input is an assumption chosen for illustration; none is a measured figure of any real service.

blocks.caption: Inputs (all assumed).

blocks.text:
#### URL shortener, step by step

- Writes per day: 100 000 000 x 0.1 = 10 000 000. Average write rate: 10^7 / 86 400 = 115.7 per second; peak 3 x 115.7 = 347 per second.
- Reads per day: 100 000 000 x 10 = 1 000 000 000. Average read rate: 11 574 per second; peak 34.7 K per second. The read-to-write ratio is 100 to 1.
- New data per day: 10^7 x 500 B = 5 GB. Over 5 years with three replicas: 5 GB x 365 x 5 x 3 = 27.4 TB.
- Peak egress: 34.7 K x 500 B x 8 = 139 Mbit/s: negligible. The system is limited by request rate, not by bandwidth.
- Cache at 20 percent of daily read bytes: 10^9 x 500 B x 0.2 = 100 GB, an upper bound; the number of distinct popular links is far smaller, so a few gigabytes per cache node suffice.

Conclusion: 35 K reads per second at peak requires several application servers and a cache tier, but 347 writes per second and 27 TB of storage fit a small sharded or even a single replicated relational deployment. The design regime is "read-heavy, cache-first".

#### Social timeline and video streaming

The timeline workload produces 231 K reads per second on average (463 K at peak) and 657 TB of replicated storage: partitioning of the data store and a cache measured in terabytes are required, and the read path (not the write path) determines the architecture. The video workload has negligible request rates (6 K views per second at peak) but 2.3 Tbit/s of peak egress and 82 PB of storage: the problem is bandwidth and bytes, which places a content delivery network and object storage at the centre. The same formulas, applied to different inputs, select three different architectures.

The following program implements the formulas above for any workload description. It was compiled and run on JDK 21 with the single-file launcher.

blocks.title: Run the estimator

blocks.text:
What to notice: the three outputs differ by orders of magnitude in different columns (request rate for the timeline, storage for the video platform, neither for the URL shortener); the `bits` helper converts bytes to bits to avoid the common error of comparing megabytes per second with megabits per second; and the cache line reports an upper bound, as explained above.

### Real-world problems and solutions

The scenarios below are composite illustrations of failure classes; the figures in them are illustrative and do not report a specific incident.

#### Problem 1: capacity sized on the average rate

**Scenario.** A service is sized for 2 000 requests per second, its daily average, with each node loaded to about 80 percent.

**Symptoms.** Latency rises every evening between 19:00 and 22:00; error rates reach several percent; scaling out after the fact takes 15 minutes.

**Diagnosis.** The request-rate graph shows an evening peak of 3.5 times the daily average, and a campaign spike reaching 8 times.

**Root cause.** The estimate omitted the peak factor, and per-node utilisation was planned at 80 percent, which leaves no headroom for variance (see the utilisation curve in the next chapter). **Fix.** Size for the observed peak hour at 50 to 60 percent utilisation, and add autoscaling with a scale-out threshold below saturation.

**Prevention.** Record the peak factor as an explicit assumption in the design document; review it against production metrics each quarter.

#### Problem 2: storage underestimated by replication, indexes and metadata

**Scenario.** A table of 5 TB of raw records is provisioned with 6 TB of disk.

**Symptoms.** The disk fills within two months; write performance degrades before the disk is full.

**Diagnosis.** The database reports 5 TB of table data, 1.8 TB of indexes, three replicas, and write-ahead log and backup retention on the same volume.

**Root cause.** The estimate counted payload bytes only. Indexes (20 to 50 percent), replication (three copies), write-ahead logs, snapshots and the free-space reserve needed for compaction or vacuuming were omitted.

**Fix.** Provision at least 2 times the logical size per copy, multiplied by the replica count; alert at 70 percent usage.

**Prevention.** The estimate table contains separate rows for payload, index overhead, replication and operational reserve.

#### Problem 3: bits and bytes confused in bandwidth planning

**Scenario.** A media endpoint is planned for a 1 Gbit/s link on the basis of "100 MB per second of peak traffic".

**Symptoms.** The link saturates at 125 MB per second of payload, but protocol overhead and retransmissions reduce usable throughput to about 110 MB per second; downloads stall at peak.

**Diagnosis.** Interface counters show sustained 940 Mbit/s.

**Root cause.** The plan treated 100 MB per second as 100 Mbit per second in one place and as 1 Gbit per second in another, and ignored overhead. 100 MB per second is 800 Mbit per second, which leaves almost no headroom on a 1 Gbit/s link.

**Fix.** Convert every figure to one unit (the estimator multiplies bytes by 8 exactly once) and plan for at most 60 to 70 percent of the nominal link rate.

**Prevention.** Record units in every row of the estimate table.

### Questions to expect

1. **1. Estimate the storage for 100 million users who each upload one 200 KB photo per day for five**

#### years.

Daily: 10^8 x 200 KB = 20 TB. Five years: 20 TB x 365 x 5 = 36.5 PB. With three replicas: about 110 PB. Thumbnails and variants add perhaps 20 to 30 percent. The answer states the assumptions (one upload per user per day is high; a typical figure may be 0.1 to 0.5) and shows that the result is dominated by retention and replication.

#### 2. Why is the peak factor applied, and how is it chosen?

Systems fail at the peak, not on average. The factor is taken from comparable systems or from measured data: a daily cycle usually gives two to three, event-driven services five or more. When no data exists, 2 to 3 is assumed and labelled.

#### 3. How many servers are required for 35 000 requests per second?

If a server sustains 1 000 requests per second at saturation and is run at 60 percent utilisation, each serves 600; 35 000 / 600 is about 58 servers, plus N+1 or N+2 redundancy and a zone failure margin, which brings the figure to about

1. The per-server capacity is an assumption to be replaced by a load-test result.

#### 4. When is a cache useful, judged from the estimate?

When the read-to-write ratio is high, when the hot working set fits in memory, and when the saving in latency or database load justifies the consistency complexity. The 80/20 observation suggests that caching 20 percent of the data may serve 80 percent of reads, which the estimate checks against the cache memory budget.

#### 5. What does a latency table teach about design?

That network round trips and disk seeks dominate, so designs minimise sequential remote calls, batch requests, keep data in memory when access is frequent, place data near users, and prefer sequential to random I/O.

#### 6. How is bandwidth estimated for a video service?

Average bitrate times concurrent viewers: for example 5 Mbit/s x 1 000 000 concurrent streams = 5 Tbit/s. The result exceeds what an origin can serve, which establishes the need for a CDN and explains why the origin sees only cache-miss traffic.

#### 7. Why are estimates rounded so aggressively?

Inputs such as daily active users are themselves uncertain by a factor of two. Precision beyond one significant digit is false precision, and rounding (86 400 to 10^5) keeps the arithmetic fast and the structure of the argument visible.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Estimation selects the design regime; a factor-of-two error rarely changes the architecture, an order-of-magnitude error does.
- Rates derive from users x actions per day / 86 400, multiplied by an assumed peak factor of 2 to 5.
- Storage = daily bytes x 365 x years x replicas, plus index, log and reserve overhead.
- Bandwidth uses bits: bytes per second x 8; plan for 60 to 70 percent link utilisation.
- Latency ratios (memory, data-center network, disk, intercontinental) explain why caches, batching and locality dominate designs; quote the table as approximate and sourced.
- Every input is an assumption and appears with its arithmetic and units.

Scalability is the ability of a system to maintain its performance targets as load grows, by adding resources at a cost that grows roughly in proportion to the load. Performance is a separate property: a system can be fast for one user and collapse at one thousand. This chapter defines the vocabulary used in every later design (throughput, latency, percentiles, utilisation), states the three quantitative laws that predict behaviour (Amdahl, Little, and the queueing utilisation curve), and demonstrates the two effects that most often surprise engineers: tail latency amplification under fan-out and the non-linear growth of response time near saturation.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Vertical and horizontal scaling

**Vertical scaling** (scale up) replaces a node with a larger one: more cores, memory or faster disks. It requires no application change, keeps data in one place and avoids distributed-systems complexity. It is bounded by the largest available machine, its cost per unit of capacity rises steeply at the top end, and a single node remains a single point of failure. **Horizontal scaling** (scale out) adds nodes behind a load balancer or partitions data across nodes. Capacity grows by adding machines, a node failure removes only a fraction of capacity, and the ceiling is far higher. The price is complexity: the application must tolerate several instances, data must be partitioned or replicated, and operations such as joins and transactions become distributed.

blocks.text:
A practical rule is to scale vertically while it is cheap and simple, and to design the application so that scaling out remains possible: stateless application tiers first, then partitioned data when a single database node is exhausted.

Scaling decomposes along three independent axes, described as the scale cube in the literature of Abbott and Fisher: cloning identical instances behind a balancer (x axis), splitting functionality into services (y axis), and splitting data by key into partitions (z axis). Stateless web tiers use the x axis; microservices use the y axis; sharded databases use the z axis. Most systems apply all three at different layers.

#### Stateless services

A service is **stateless** when the response to a request depends only on the request and on external shared state, never on data held in the memory of a particular instance from earlier requests. Statelessness is the property that makes horizontal scaling of the application tier trivial: any instance can serve any request, so instances can be added, removed and replaced at will, and a failed instance loses nothing that cannot be recovered.

blocks.text:
Session state is the common offender. Three remedies exist: store the session in a shared, replicated store (an in-memory data store is typical), carry the state in the client in a signed or encrypted token (a JSON Web Token, as covered in the Spring Security material), or keep the server stateful and route by affinity, which accepts the failure and rebalancing problems described in the next chapter. Other instance-local state to be removed includes uploaded files on local disk, in-memory caches that must be consistent across instances, and scheduled jobs that run once per instance instead of once per cluster.

#### Throughput, latency and response time

**Throughput** is the number of operations completed per unit of time (requests per second, megabytes per second). **Latency** is the time one operation takes. **Response time**, as the client observes it, equals service time (the time the resource spends working on the request) plus waiting time (queueing) plus network time. Throughput and latency are related but distinct: a pipeline can have high throughput and high latency (a batch job), or low latency and low throughput (a single request on an idle machine). The targets in a design are stated for both, for example "40 K requests per second at p99 below 200 ms".

#### Percentiles and why averages mislead

The mean of a latency distribution hides its tail. A service with a mean of 50 ms may answer 99 percent of requests in 30 ms and one percent in 2 seconds. Percentiles state the distribution directly: **p50** (the median) is the typical case, **p95** and **p99** are the experience of the slowest 5 and 1 percent of requests, and **p99.9** captures rarer events. The Google SRE book states a general preference for percentiles over the mean, because averages hide long-tail behaviour while high percentiles show the plausible worst case.

Percentiles of different requests do not combine by averaging, and percentiles per node cannot be averaged into a cluster percentile; the underlying histograms must be merged. A single page view typically issues many requests, so a user meets a slow response far more often than the per-request percentile suggests: with 20 requests per page and 1 percent of requests slow, the probability that a page includes at least one slow request is 1 - 0.99^20 = 18 percent.

#### Tail latency amplification

The effect above compounds in services that fan out. When one request needs the answers of N backend calls issued in parallel, the request completes when the slowest call completes. If each call is slow with probability q, the probability that at least one of N calls is slow is 1 - (1 - q)^N. Dean and Barroso describe the case of a server that answers within one second 99 percent of the time: when a request must collect responses from 100 such servers, about 63 percent of user requests take more than one second ("The Tail at Scale", Communications of the ACM, 2013; the figure follows from 1 - 0.99^100).

Return what has arrived by the deadline
Send a second copy of the request to another replica if no reply arrives within the p95 latency; use the first reply
About 5 percent extra load when deferred to p95 (per Dean and Barroso)
Send to two replicas at once, each told of the other, so the second cancels when the first starts

Separate queues for interactive and batch work

blocks.caption: Mitigations for tail latency.

blocks.text:
#### Amdahl's law

Amdahl's law bounds the speedup obtainable by parallelising a task. If a fraction p of the work can run in parallel and the rest (1 - p) is serial, then the speedup on n workers is 1 / ((1 - p) + p / n), and the limit as n grows is 1 / (1 - p). A task that is 95 percent parallel can never run more than 20 times faster, regardless of the number of workers, and 32 workers achieve only 12.6 times.

blocks.caption: Speedup curves for four parallel fractions; the serial fraction (a lock, a single database primary, a shared counter) sets the plateau, so removing the serial portion matters more than adding workers.
blocks.alt: Amdahl speedup versus number of workers | 60 | p = 0.99 | 50 | 40 | 30 | 20 | p = 0.95 | 10 p = 0.90 | p = 0.50 | 0 | 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 | workers n (log scale)

blocks.text:
In system design the serial fraction appears as any resource that every request must pass through: a single database primary, a global lock, a leader that sequences writes, a shared counter. The law also underestimates the real cost, because adding workers introduces coordination overhead (contention and coherence delays); the Universal Scalability Law of Neil Gunther extends the model with a term for it, which explains why throughput can decrease when too many workers contend for one resource.

#### Little's law

Little's law states that in a stable system the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate multiplied by the average time each item spends in the system:

**Little's law**

blocks.code:
L = lambda x W
L      average number of requests in the system (in flight)
lambda average arrival rate (requests per second)
W      average time in the system (seconds), queueing plus service

blocks.text:
The law holds for any stable system regardless of the arrival or service distributions, which makes it the most useful sizing identity in practice. It converts a latency and a rate into a concurrency, and concurrency determines thread counts, connection pool sizes and memory.

#### Queueing and the utilisation curve

Requests wait when they arrive faster than they are served. For the simplest model of one server with random (Poisson) arrivals and exponentially distributed service times, called M/M/1, the mean time in the system is W = S / (1 - rho), where S is the mean service time and rho is the utilisation (arrival rate divided by capacity). The mean response time is 2 S at 50 percent utilisation, 5 S at 80 percent, 10 S at 90 percent, and 100 S at 99 percent. Response time does not grow in proportion to load; it grows without bound as utilisation approaches 100 percent.

blocks.caption: Mean response time of an M/M/1 queue with 10 ms service time; the knee begins near 70 to 80 percent utilisation, so capacity planning targets 50 to 70 percent at peak.
blocks.alt: M/M/1 mean response time versus utilisation (service time 10 ms) | 968 ms | 1000 | line: formula dots: simulation | 750 | 500 | 250 201 ms | 100 ms | 50 ms | 20 ms | 0 | 0 % 20 % 40 % 60 % 80 % 100 % | utilisation (arrival rate / capacity)

blocks.text:
Real systems are not M/M/1 (service times have heavier tails, requests arrive in bursts, there are several servers per queue), so the curve is a qualitative guide. The conclusions are robust: a system close to saturation has high and unstable latency, a small increase in load produces a large increase in response time, and capacity must include headroom. Several servers sharing one queue (M/M/c) wait less than the same capacity split into separate queues, which is an argument for balancing requests to the least loaded node.

### Worked example

The following computations use only the formulas above, with assumed inputs.

#### Sizing concurrency with Little's law

A service receives 35 000 requests per second at peak (the page-view counter of the previous chapter) and each request takes 50 ms on average. In-flight requests: L = 35 000 x 0.050 = 1 750. If one node runs 100 concurrent request handlers (assumed), 1 750 / 100 = 17.5, so 18 nodes at full concurrency and 30 nodes at 60 percent target utilisation. If each request holds a database connection for 5 ms, the average number of busy connections across the fleet is 35 000 x 0.005 = 175; a pool of 20 connections per node over 30 nodes (600 connections) is sufficient on average, but the database must accept 600 connections, which is itself a constraint to check.

A converse use: a database client pool of 20 connections and a mean query time of 5 ms cannot sustain more than 20 / 0.005 = 4 000 queries per second, whatever the number of application threads. Raising the thread count without raising the pool only lengthens the queue.

#### Predicting the benefit of parallelism

A report job takes 60 minutes; 10 percent of it (reading the input, writing the final file) is serial. With 8 workers the time is 60 x (0.10 + 0.90 / 8) = 60 x 0.2125 = 12.75 minutes, a speedup of 4.7 (the table value for p = 0.90, n = 8). With 32 workers: 60 x (0.10 + 0.9 / 32) = 7.7 minutes, a speedup of 7.8. Quadrupling the workers from 8 to 32 saves five minutes; halving the serial part from 10 to 5 percent saves 2.6 minutes at 8 workers (12.75 to 10.1 minutes) without adding any worker.

### Hands-on: tail latency and queueing, simulated

Both programs below were run on JDK 21 (single-file launcher). They are single-machine simulations of the formulas, not measurements of any real service.

#### Tail amplification

Each simulated backend call has a lognormal body (median 10 ms) and a 1 percent chance of an additional stall of 100 to 300 ms. A request issues N calls in parallel and completes with the slowest. 200 000 requests are simulated per N.

The backend that is "fast 99 percent of the time" produces a service that is slow most of the time at a fan-out of 100.

#### Queueing and Amdahl

blocks.text:
What to notice: the simulated mean and p99 follow the formulas W = S / (1 - rho) and p99 = W x ln(100) (the response time of an M/M/1 queue is exponentially distributed); at 90 percent utilisation the mean is already 100 ms for a 10 ms service time; the simulated value at 99 percent is below the formula because a finite sample of two million requests does not fully reach the slowly converging steady state; and the last column confirms Little's law (L = lambda x W) in every row. The Amdahl table reproduces the speedups quoted above.

### Real-world problems and solutions

The scenarios below are composite illustrations of failure classes; the figures in them are illustrative and do not report a specific incident.

#### Problem 1: tail latency from fan-out

**Scenario.** A product page assembles its content from 40 backend calls (pricing, inventory, reviews, recommendations and others) issued in parallel. Each backend meets its own objective of p99 below 100 ms.

**Symptoms.** The page p50 is acceptable, but about one page in three exceeds one second; backend dashboards show every individual service healthy.

**Diagnosis.** Per-service p99 is within objective. The page latency histogram has a long right tail. With 40 calls and a 1 percent slow probability per call, the expected fraction of pages containing a slow call is 1 - 0.99^40 = 33 percent.

**Root cause.** Latency of a fan-out request is the maximum of its calls, so per-service percentiles understate page percentiles; the objective was applied at the wrong level.

**Fix.** Set per-call objectives from the page objective (the per-call tail must be much rarer than 1 percent); add a per-call deadline with a degraded default for non-essential calls (render without recommendations); hedge idempotent reads after the p95 latency; reduce the number of calls through aggregation.

**Prevention.** Define SLOs at the user-visible request level, and alert on end-to-end percentiles, not on per-service averages.

#### Problem 2: the application tier scales, the database does not

**Scenario.** Application servers are autoscaled from 10 to 40 nodes during a traffic increase.

**Symptoms.** Throughput stops increasing at 25 nodes; latency rises; the database reports a large number of waiting connections and CPU near 95 percent; application logs show connection acquisition timeouts.

**Diagnosis.** The database primary is saturated; each added application node adds connections and load to it, and the connection limit is reached (40 nodes x 30 connections = 1 200 against a limit of 500).

**Root cause.** The shared stateful tier is the serial fraction of Amdahl's law; adding stateless nodes cannot raise throughput beyond what the database sustains and may lower it through connection overhead.

**Fix.** Cap total connections with a pooler placed in front of the database, add read replicas for read traffic, cache frequent reads, and batch writes; raise the database capacity or partition it when the single node is the limit.

**Prevention.** Load-test the whole path, locate the first saturating resource, and compute connection budgets per tier from Little's law before scaling out.

#### Problem 3: local state blocks scale-in and failover

**Scenario.** An application stores shopping-cart contents in the memory of the node that created the session; the balancer uses cookie affinity.

**Symptoms.** Users report empty carts after deployments and after the autoscaler removes nodes at night; one node carries a disproportionate share of long sessions.

**Diagnosis.** Carts disappear exactly when the owning node is replaced or removed; per-node memory differs by a factor of three.

**Root cause.** Session data lives in instance memory, so the node cannot be removed without destroying state and affinity distributes load by session count, not by work.

**Fix.** Move the cart to a replicated shared store keyed by session or user identifier, with a time-to-live; keep nodes stateless.

**Prevention.** A design review rule: no durable or semi-durable state in an application instance; instances must be disposable.

#### Problem 4: averages hide an overloaded service

**Scenario.** An alert is configured on mean latency above 300 ms; the mean is 120 ms.

**Symptoms.** Customer complaints about timeouts continue while dashboards are green.

**Diagnosis.** The p99 latency is 4.5 seconds; 2 percent of requests time out at the client.

**Root cause.** The mean is dominated by the fast majority and conceals a slow tail caused by queueing at a saturated shard.

**Fix.** Alert on p99 (and on error and timeout rates), segment latency by shard and endpoint, and add load shedding on the saturated shard.

**Prevention.** SLIs defined as percentiles over a fixed window (see the availability chapter).

### Questions to expect

#### 1. Compare vertical and horizontal scaling.

Vertical scaling enlarges one node: simple, no distribution problems, but bounded, expensive at the top end and a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling adds nodes: higher ceiling, fault tolerant, but requires statelessness, partitioning and coordination. A typical path is vertical first, then stateless horizontal scaling of the application tier, then read replicas and partitioning of the database.

#### 2. What makes a service stateless, and why does it matter?

No request depends on instance-local memory from earlier requests; durable and session state live in shared stores or in client-held tokens. Any instance can handle any request, so instances can be added, removed, restarted and load-balanced without coordination or data loss.

#### 3. Why are percentiles preferred to the average?

The average conceals the tail and mixes populations; percentiles describe what a given fraction of users experience. Users experience many requests per session, so the tail is encountered often. Percentiles must be computed from merged histograms and cannot be averaged across nodes.

1. **4. A request fans out to 50 services, each with p99 of 100 ms. What is the probability the request**

#### exceeds 100 ms?

If calls are independent and each exceeds 100 ms with probability 0.01, the request exceeds 100 ms when at least one call does: 1 - 0.99^50 = 39.5 percent. Mitigations are fewer calls, deadlines with partial results, and hedged requests.

#### 5. State Little's law and give a use.

L = lambda x W: the average number in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time in the system. Use: 10 000 requests per second at 100 ms average latency implies 1 000 requests in flight, which sizes thread pools and connection pools.

#### 6. Why does latency rise sharply as utilisation approaches 100 percent?

In a queue, arrivals sometimes bunch together and the server cannot catch up; the waiting time grows as 1 / (1 - utilisation) in the M/M/1 model, so going from 90 to 99 percent utilisation multiplies the mean response time by ten. Capacity plans keep peak utilisation near 50 to 70 percent.

#### 7. What does Amdahl's law imply for scaling a service?

The serial portion (one database primary, a global lock, a sequencer) bounds the benefit of adding workers: with 5 percent serial work the speedup is capped at 20. Effort is better spent shrinking the serial portion (partitioning the data, removing the lock) than adding nodes.

#### 8. What is a hedged request and when is it safe?

A hedged request sends a duplicate of an in-progress request to a second replica after a delay near the p95 latency and uses whichever answer arrives first. It is safe for idempotent reads, adds a small amount of load (about 5 percent when the delay is p95), and sharply reduces tail latency. Non-idempotent writes need an idempotency key first.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Scale out when the application is stateless; the shared stateful tier then becomes the limit (Amdahl) and is scaled by replicas, caches and partitioning.
- State targets as throughput plus a percentile latency; use merged histograms, never averages of percentiles.
- Fan-out multiplies tail risk: P(slow) = 1 - (1 - q)^N; reduce fan-out, set deadlines, hedge idempotent calls.
- Little's law L = lambda x W sizes concurrency, thread pools and connection pools.
- Queueing delay grows as 1 / (1 - utilisation); plan 50 to 70 percent utilisation at peak.
- Simulations on one machine illustrate formulas; real capacity is established by load testing the real system.

sections.title: Load Balancing and Networking for Design

blocks.text:
A load balancer distributes incoming work across a pool of servers so that no single server is overloaded, failed servers are bypassed, and capacity can be added or removed without clients noticing. Together with DNS, content delivery networks, reverse proxies and API gateways it forms the network edge of almost every system in this book. The problems it solves are three: capacity (one server cannot serve the load), availability (one failed server must not cause an outage) and operability (servers must be replaceable during deployment without dropping requests).

This chapter covers the layers at which balancing happens, the algorithms and their measured behaviour in a simulation, health checking, session affinity, connection draining, and the surrounding components (DNS, GeoDNS, CDN, anycast, reverse proxy, gateway). The operating-system and TCP details that underlie these components are covered in the computer networks material and are not repeated.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Where balancing happens

blocks.caption: A typical request path: DNS or anycast steers the client to an edge; a CDN and web application firewall absorb static and hostile traffic; a layer 4 balancer spreads connections over a gateway tier that authenticates, rate-limits and routes to services, each owning its data.
blocks.alt: API gateway tier | DNS / CDN L4 LB | Clients TLS termination | anycast + WAF (NLB-style) | authn / authz | rate limiting | routing + retries | Internal | Orders Catalog Users Search | calls via service service service service | sidecar or | client LB | Orders DB Catalog DB Users DB Index

blocks.text:
Balancing occurs at several layers, and large systems use several at once:

- **DNS** returns different addresses for the same name (round robin, weighted, or geography-aware answers).
- **Network edge**: anycast addresses and CDN points of presence terminate client connections near the user.
- **Layer 4 balancer** forwards TCP or UDP connections without interpreting the application protocol.
- **Layer 7 balancer, reverse proxy and API gateway** terminate TLS and HTTP and route by request contents.
- **Client-side or sidecar balancing** places the decision inside the calling service (a client library or a service-mesh proxy), which removes one network hop for internal calls; Spring Cloud LoadBalancer is the Java example covered in the Spring microservices material.

#### Layer 4 versus layer 7

blocks.text: A layer 4 balancer operates on the transport layer. It selects a backend when a connection starts and then forwards every packet of that connection to it, so one TCP connection always reaches one server. It is fast, handles any protocol on top of TCP or UDP (databases, message brokers, TLS passthrough), and needs little CPU per connection. A layer 7 balancer operates on the application layer. It terminates the client connection, parses HTTP, selects a backend per request and opens or reuses a separate connection to that backend. It can route by hostname or path, terminate TLS, retry idempotent requests, add headers, compress, enforce authentication and balance the many requests that share one long-lived HTTP/2 connection.

rows: One backend per connection for its lifetime
One backend per request, even on a shared connection
Passthrough, or terminated at the balancer by some products
Terminated at the balancer; backends may receive plain or re-encrypted traffic
Very high connection rate, low latency, static client address preserved by some products
Path and host routing, retries, rate limiting, authentication, header manipulation, observability per route
Higher CPU and latency per request
Cloud network balancers; HAProxy in TCP mode; IPVS
Cloud application balancers; NGINX; Envoy; HAProxy in HTTP mode
blocks.caption: Layer 4 compared with layer 7.

blocks.text:
The AWS documentation illustrates the distinction. The Network Load Balancer selects a target by a flow hash over protocol, source and destination address and port, and TCP sequence number, and routes each TCP connection to a single target for its lifetime. The Application Load Balancer evaluates listener rules in priority order and then selects a target from the chosen target group, with round robin as the default algorithm (per the AWS Elastic Load Balancing documentation).

The consequence for design: an HTTP/2 or gRPC client typically keeps one long-lived connection and multiplexes many requests on it. A layer 4 balancer sees one connection and therefore sends all the requests of that client to one backend; a layer 7 balancer can spread them. This matters for gRPC services in particular.

#### Balancing algorithms

rows: Cycle through backends; weights give larger nodes more turns
Many independent balancers; simple, no shared state
Send to the backend with the fewest in-flight requests
Requests of variable duration; heterogeneous or degrading backends
Sample two backends at random; send to the one with fewer in-flight requests
Many balancers without a global view; near-optimal balancing with O(1) work
Hash on a key (source address, session, URL, user)
The key determines the backend; consistent hashing keeps most assignments stable when the pool changes
Cache affinity, session locality, sharded state
Prefer the backend with lower measured response time
Backends with variable speed; requires measurement
blocks.caption: Common algorithms.

blocks.text: **Least connections** reacts to actual load, because a slow server accumulates in-flight requests and receives fewer new ones. Its weakness is that an accurate count requires a single balancer (or shared state), and a failing server that returns errors instantly appears to have few connections and attracts traffic.

blocks.text:
**Power of two choices** (P2C) obtains most of the benefit of least connections without a global scan. Envoy documents this as its default least-request behaviour when host weights are equal: it selects N random available hosts (2 by default) and picks the one with the fewest active requests. NGINX offers the same idea as `random two least_conn`, which randomly picks two servers and then applies `least_conn` between them (both per the respective documentation).

**Hash-based balancing** maps a key to a backend. With simple modulo hashing, changing the number of backends from N to N+1 moves almost all keys. **Consistent hashing** places both backends and keys on a ring so that a change moves only about 1/(N+1) of the keys, which preserves cache contents and session locality; NGINX documents `hash` `key consistent` as ketama consistent hashing, and Envoy offers ring hash and Maglev policies. The ring construction, virtual nodes and rebalancing are treated in the chapter on replication, partitioning and consistent hashing; the demonstration in this chapter measures only the remapping effect. A hash policy balances well only if the keys are spread evenly: popular keys concentrate on one backend (see the hot instance problem below).

#### Health checks

A balancer must stop sending traffic to a failed backend. Two mechanisms are combined. **Passive checks** observe real traffic: after a number of failed requests within a window the backend is marked unavailable for a period (NGINX open source: `max_fails` defaults to 1 and `fail_timeout` to 10 seconds, per its documentation). **Active checks** probe a health endpoint periodically; NGINX documents periodic active health checks as part of its commercial subscription, while HAProxy, Envoy and the cloud balancers provide them natively.

The design of the health endpoint matters more than the mechanism:

- A **liveness** check answers "is the process running". A **readiness** check answers "can this instance serve traffic now" (dependencies connected, caches warmed, migrations finished). Balancers use readiness; restart logic uses liveness. Kubernetes liveness and readiness probes encode the same distinction.
- A **shallow** check (return 200) detects a crashed process only. A **deep** check that queries the database detects a broken dependency but can make every instance appear unhealthy at once when the shared dependency fails, so the balancer removes the whole pool and converts a partial degradation into a total outage. A common compromise is a deep check for dependencies local to the instance and a shallow check for shared ones, with the shared dependency failure handled by the application (degradation, circuit breaker).
- Thresholds trade detection speed for stability: for example mark down after 3 consecutive failures at 5-second intervals (about 15 seconds), and mark up after 2 consecutive successes. Aggressive thresholds cause flapping.

#### Session affinity (sticky sessions)

Affinity pins a client to one backend, by source address hash, by a cookie inserted by the balancer, or by an application session identifier. It is used when instances hold session state or local caches. The costs are uneven load (heavy users stay on one node), loss of the session when that node fails or is replaced, and difficulty in scaling in. Statelessness (see the previous chapter) is the preferred remedy; affinity remains legitimate for connection-oriented protocols such as WebSockets, where the connection itself is the unit of stickiness, and for cache locality, where a soft preference through consistent hashing is preferable to a hard pin.

#### Connection draining

Removing a backend must not break requests in flight. **Connection draining** (also called deregistration delay or graceful shutdown) marks the backend as no longer eligible for new requests while it completes the existing ones, up to a timeout, after which it is terminated.

blocks.text:
The sequence has three timing requirements. The drain timeout must exceed the longest normal request (otherwise long requests are cut). The application must handle SIGTERM by stopping its listener and finishing in-flight work, which Spring Boot supports through graceful shutdown (`server.shutdown=graceful`, with `spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase` for the grace period). The orchestrator must not send SIGKILL before the application has finished, so its termination grace period exceeds drain plus shutdown work.

#### DNS, GeoDNS, CDN, reverse proxy, gateway and anycast

blocks.text:
**DNS-based balancing** returns several addresses for one name, or different addresses by policy. It is the only mechanism that works before a connection exists, and it directs users to a region. Its limits are caching (resolvers and clients keep answers for the record time-to-live, so a failover takes at least one TTL plus the behaviour of non-compliant resolvers), no knowledge of connection load, and coarse granularity. TTLs of 30 to 60 seconds are common for records that must fail over, at the price of more resolver traffic. **GeoDNS** (geolocation or latency-based routing) answers according to the resolver location or, where supported, the client subnet, so that users reach the nearest region; the decision is based on the resolver, which may be far from the user.

**Anycast** announces the same IP address from several locations through the routing protocol (BGP); packets reach the topologically nearest location. It is used by public DNS services and CDNs. A routing change can move a client to another location in the middle of a TCP connection, so anycast suits short-lived connections and stateless protocols best, or must be combined with connection handling at the edge.

A **CDN** caches content at points of presence near users. Static assets and cacheable API responses are served from the edge, which removes both latency (the round trip to the origin) and origin load; the cache header details belong to the caching chapter. A **shield** or regional tier collapses misses from many edges into one request to the origin.

A **reverse proxy** sits in front of servers and forwards client requests to them, adding TLS termination, compression, caching, connection pooling to backends and request buffering that protects slow application servers from slow clients. An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy with API-management features: authentication and authorisation, rate limiting, request routing and transformation, versioning, and aggregated telemetry. It is the usual single entry point of a microservice system; the corresponding Spring component is Spring Cloud Gateway. A gateway centralises cross-cutting concerns, at the price of becoming a critical component that must itself be redundant and kept free of business logic.

### Worked example

A service must handle 35 000 requests per second at peak, with a mean response of 50 ms (the sizing of the previous chapter, 1 750 requests in flight). The edge is designed as follows (all capacity figures assumed).

rows: 35 K requests per second, assume 3 requests per connection at peak: about 12 K new connections per second; a single managed or software balancer handles this class of load
Assume 5 000 requests per second per gateway node with TLS termination and auth at 60 percent target utilisation: 35 000 / 3 000 = 11.7 nodes
1 750 in flight, 100 concurrent per node at 60 percent: 1 750 / 60
Losing one zone removes 33 percent of capacity: the remaining 20 nodes must carry 35 000 requests per second at 100 concurrency each = 2 000 in flight (above 1 750)
Sizing is adequate, with no headroom; add 3 to 5 nodes
blocks.caption: Edge sizing (assumed capacities).

blocks.text:
The last row demonstrates the rule used throughout this book: capacity is checked for the failure of the largest failure domain, not only for the healthy case.

### Hands-on: balancing algorithms simulated

The simulation models ten backends. Each backend is a single-server FIFO queue; request service times are lognormal (median 8 ms, mean about 11 ms); arrivals are Poisson. 400 000 requests are simulated per algorithm. Scenario A has ten equal backends at 700 requests per second (the pool capacity is about 900 per second). Scenario B has one backend (node 0) three times slower, at 500 requests per second. Hash-based routing uses 10 000 keys with a Zipf popularity distribution (exponent 1), a realistic shape for popular content, on a ring of 150 virtual nodes per backend. This is a one-process simulation of queueing behaviour, not a benchmark of any real balancer.

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- In scenario A, all four load-based algorithms spread requests evenly (node 0 receives 10 percent), but the p99 differs: 64 ms for least connections, 88 ms for power of two choices, 143 ms for round robin and 223 ms for random. Random placement creates transient imbalance; round robin removes count imbalance but ignores the variable duration of requests.
- In scenario B, round robin and random send 10 percent of the traffic (50 requests per second) to a node whose capacity is about 30 per second, so its queue grows without bound; the p99 in the output (hundreds of seconds) is a property of the run length and only shows that the system is unstable. Least connections reduces the share of the slow node to 4.8 percent and power of two choices to 5.4 percent, and both keep the p99 near 70 to 110 ms.
- The key-hash policy concentrates traffic: with Zipf-skewed keys two nodes receive 19.7 and 17.2 percent of the requests, the busiest node receives 1.97 times the mean, and the p99 explodes. Hash routing is appropriate for cache or state locality, not as a general-purpose balancing algorithm for skewed keys.

blocks.title: Run

blocks.text:
Modulo hashing moves 84 to 95 percent of the keys when one node is added, while the ring moves almost exactly the ideal fraction 1/(N+1). For a cache tier this is the difference between losing a sixth of the cached data and losing nearly all of it, which would send the full read load to the database.

### Real-world problems and solutions

The scenarios below are composite illustrations of failure classes; the figures in them are illustrative and do not report a specific incident.

#### Problem 1: sticky-session imbalance

**Scenario.** A web application uses cookie-based affinity with 6 nodes. Users stay logged in for hours; a small fraction are power users with many requests.

**Symptoms.** One node runs at 90 percent CPU while the others are at 35 percent; p99 latency is high for the users pinned to that node; the autoscaler adds nodes, but the new nodes receive few sessions.

**Diagnosis.** Per-node request counts diverge; the busy node holds the longest-lived and heaviest sessions; new nodes only receive newly created sessions.

**Root cause.** Affinity assigns sessions, not work, at login time and never rebalances; session length and request rate vary by orders of magnitude.

**Fix.** Externalise session state so that any node can serve any request and disable affinity; if affinity is required for caches, use consistent hashing with a bounded load (a node above a threshold sheds to the next one); cap session lifetime so that sessions redistribute.

**Prevention.** Alert on the ratio of the maximum to the mean per-node load; require a design justification for any hard affinity.

#### Problem 2: an unhealthy node still receives traffic

**Scenario.** One of eight nodes loses its connection to the database but its process keeps running; the health endpoint returns 200 because it checks only the process.

**Symptoms.** About one request in eight fails with a 500 error; the error rate persists for hours; the node's CPU is low (it fails quickly).

**Diagnosis.** Errors cluster on one instance in logs and traces; the balancer shows all targets healthy.

**Root cause.** The health check does not reflect the ability to serve; additionally, with least connections the node attracts more traffic than its share because failed requests finish fast and keep its in-flight count low.

**Fix.** Use a readiness check that verifies the dependencies the instance owns; add passive outlier detection that ejects a node whose error rate exceeds a threshold (with a cap on the ejected fraction so that a global failure does not eject everything); prefer algorithms that account for errors, such as peak EWMA with failure penalties.

**Prevention.** Chaos tests that break one instance's dependency and verify its removal within the intended time.

#### Problem 3: hot instance under skewed keys

**Scenario.** A cache tier routes by hash of the key. One celebrity profile receives 8 percent of all reads.

**Symptoms.** One cache node saturates its network interface and CPU; cache latency rises for all keys on that node; the hit rate of the pool appears normal.

**Diagnosis.** Per-node request rate shows one node at roughly two times the mean (as in the simulation above: 1.97); a key-level top-N report identifies a single key.

**Root cause.** Hash routing assigns every request for a key to one node, so popularity skew becomes load skew; adding nodes does not divide a single key.

**Fix.** Replicate hot keys across several nodes and read from a random replica; add a small local in-process cache with a short TTL in front for the hottest keys; split the key (append a random suffix on write to several sub-keys, read from any).

**Prevention.** Monitor top-key frequency; load-test with skewed key distributions, not only uniform ones.

#### Problem 4: thundering herd after restart

**Scenario.** After a deployment or an incident, every node of a service restarts at about the same time. Caches are cold, connection pools are empty and the JVM has not yet compiled hot paths.

**Symptoms.** Immediately after the restart the first nodes marked healthy receive their full share, or more (a least-connections balancer favours a node with zero connections); latency and errors spike; nodes crash again and the cycle repeats.

**Diagnosis.** Error rate correlates with node start time; the database sees a burst of identical queries and connection attempts.

**Root cause.** Newly started nodes receive full traffic instantly although their effective capacity is a fraction of normal, and cold caches turn every request into a database query.

**Fix.** Ramp traffic up gradually (slow start: the balancer raises the weight of a new node over a period; NGINX documents `slow_start`, noting it as a commercial feature; Envoy and cloud balancers offer comparable options), warm up caches and connections before reporting ready, stagger restarts (rolling updates with a small surge), and add jitter to client reconnect and refresh timers.

**Prevention.** Rolling deployments with readiness gates and a maximum unavailable percentage; load-test the cold-start path.

#### Problem 5: the balancer as a single point of failure

**Scenario.** All traffic enters through one load balancer instance.

**Symptoms.** A host failure, a software upgrade or a saturated network interface takes the whole service offline.

**Diagnosis.** The balancer appears at the root of every dependency graph; no standby exists or failover is manual.

**Root cause.** Redundancy was applied to the servers but not to the component that fronts them.

**Fix.** Run at least two balancers in active-active (with DNS or anycast spreading clients) or active-passive with a floating address and a health-checked failover; use a managed balancer that is itself distributed across zones.

**Prevention.** A design checklist of every component on the request path, each with its failure behaviour (see the chapter on availability and reliability).

### Questions to expect

#### 1. What is the difference between a layer 4 and a layer 7 load balancer?

Layer 4 balances connections using addresses and ports, is fast and protocol-agnostic, and pins a connection to one backend. Layer 7 terminates the application protocol and balances individual requests by URL, header or cookie, enabling path routing, retries, TLS termination and authentication, at higher cost. For multiplexed protocols such as HTTP/2 and gRPC, layer 7 is needed to spread the requests of one connection.

#### 2. Which algorithm is selected for requests of very different duration?

Least connections (least outstanding requests) or power of two choices, because they react to actual load. Round robin ignores the duration and lets slow requests accumulate on a node. P2C obtains nearly the same result as least connections without needing a global view across multiple balancers.

#### 3. Why does consistent hashing matter for a cache tier?

Modulo hashing remaps almost all keys when the node count changes (84 to 95 percent in the measurement above), flushing the effective cache and flooding the database. Consistent hashing remaps about 1/(N+1) of the keys.

#### 4. How are failed servers detected, and what are the pitfalls?

By passive checks (observed errors) and active probes of a health endpoint. Pitfalls: a shallow check that misses broken dependencies; a deep check that removes the whole pool when a shared dependency fails; flapping from aggressive thresholds; and no cap on ejection.

#### 5. When are sticky sessions acceptable?

For connection-oriented protocols (WebSockets), and for cache locality where a soft preference suffices. For HTTP sessions, externalising state is preferable because affinity causes imbalance and loses sessions on failure.

#### 6. What happens to in-flight requests when an instance is removed during deployment?

With connection draining, the balancer stops sending new requests, the instance completes in-flight work within a timeout, and only then terminates. Without it, in-flight requests are cut and clients see errors. The application must handle SIGTERM gracefully and the grace period must exceed the longest request.

#### 7. How does DNS-based failover behave, and why is it slow?

The authoritative server stops returning the failed address, but resolvers and clients cache the old answer for the TTL, and some ignore low TTLs. Failover therefore takes at least the TTL, often longer. Faster failover uses anycast, a floating address or a balancer in front, with DNS used for regional steering.

#### 8. What is the role of an API gateway, and what are its risks?

It centralises authentication, rate limiting, routing, request transformation and telemetry at the entry point. Risks: it becomes a critical, high-traffic component requiring redundancy; it may accumulate business logic; and it adds a network hop. It is kept thin and stateless.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Layer 4 balances connections quickly; layer 7 balances requests with rich policy; multiplexed protocols need layer 7 to spread load.
- Least connections and power of two choices adapt to variable work and slow nodes (simulated p99 of 64 and 88 ms against 143 and 223 ms for round robin and random); hash routing serves locality, not even balance.
- Consistent hashing remaps about 1/(N+1) of keys on a pool change; modulo hashing remaps 84 to 95 percent in the measurement.
- Health checks must reflect the ability to serve without letting a shared dependency empty the pool; draining and graceful shutdown protect in-flight requests.
- DNS failover is bounded by the TTL; anycast and floating addresses fail over faster; every component on the request path, including the balancer, needs redundancy.
- Capacity is verified for the loss of a whole failure domain, not only for the healthy case.

A system that is fast but frequently unavailable has no value to its users, and a system that is available but returns wrong results has negative value. **Availability** is the fraction of time (or of requests) for which a service performs its function correctly. **Reliability** is the probability that the service performs correctly for a stated period under stated conditions; it includes correctness and durability as well as uptime. Designs achieve both by assuming that every component fails, in every possible way, and by arranging redundancy, isolation and graceful behaviour so that individual failures do not become user-visible outages.

This chapter defines the vocabulary of service-level objectives, derives the arithmetic of redundancy, describes failure domains and failover, summarises the defensive techniques that Spring and the resilience material treat in code (timeouts, retries, circuit breakers), and adds the two mechanisms that protect a service from overload: backpressure and load shedding. Two simulations quantify the arithmetic of series and parallel components and the amplification caused by retries.

### Concept and mechanism

#### SLI, SLO and SLA

The Google SRE book defines the terms as follows (chapter "Service Level Objectives"). A **service level indicator** **(SLI)** is a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service that is provided. A **service** **level objective (SLO)** is a target value or range of values for a service level that is measured by an SLI. A **service** **level agreement (SLA)** is an explicit or implicit contract with users that includes consequences of meeting or missing the SLOs it contains, often financial. The relation is: SLIs are measured, SLOs are targets set internally (stricter than the SLA), and SLAs are commitments with penalties.

Typical SLIs are the fraction of requests that succeed (availability SLI), the fraction served faster than a threshold (latency SLI, for example "99 percent of requests complete in under 300 ms"), and for data systems the fraction of data that is fresh or durable. Measuring availability as the ratio of good requests to total requests over a window is more informative than measuring server uptime, because a server can be "up" and still fail every request. An **error budget** is the allowed unreliability, 1 minus the SLO. An SLO of 99.9 percent over 30 days permits 0.1 percent of requests (or 43.2 minutes of full outage) to fail. The SRE book recommends tracking the budget daily or weekly and letting its consumption inform release decisions: while budget remains, the team ships features; when it is exhausted, the team prioritises reliability work. The mechanism turns reliability from a feeling into a quantity that product and engineering share.

#### The nines

rows: Two nines: internal tools, batch systems
Three nines: common target for business services
Five nines: requires multi-region design and no manual step
