blocks.text:
Each additional nine shortens the budget tenfold. Between three and four nines the practical difference is that human detection and response (several minutes at best) no longer fit in the budget, so detection, failover and rollback must be automated. Availability promised to customers should be lower than what the architecture can deliver: the measurable availability of a service never exceeds the product of the availabilities of the components it depends on in series.

#### The arithmetic of availability

Availability of a repairable component follows from its mean time between failures (MTBF) and mean time to repair (MTTR): A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR). A component that fails once a month (MTBF about 720 hours) and takes 30 minutes to recover is available 720 / 720.5 = 99.93 percent of the time. The formula shows two levers: fail less often, or recover faster; for most systems shortening recovery time is cheaper than preventing every failure.

Components combine in two basic ways.

- **Series** (every component is needed): A = A1 x A2 x ... x An. Availability is lower than that of the weakest component, and falls with each added dependency. Five components of 99.9 percent give 0.999^5 = 99.50 percent (about 43.7 hours of downtime per year); ten give 99.0 percent.
- **Parallel** (any one component suffices): A = 1 - (1 - A1)(1 - A2)...(1 - An). Two independent replicas of 99 percent each give 1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99 percent, three give 99.9999 percent.

blocks.text:
The parallel formula assumes independent failures. Real replicas share causes: a power feed, a network switch, a software version, a configuration push, a dependency. If both replicas sit in one zone with availability 99.9 percent, the combined availability cannot exceed 99.9 percent however many replicas exist. This is the argument for spreading replicas across independent failure domains, and for diversity in deployment (staged rollout) so that one bad change does not hit every replica simultaneously. A further condition on the parallel formula is capacity: if the survivors cannot carry the full load, the replicas are not truly redundant. The standard notation is N+1 (one spare) or N+2.

#### Failure domains

A **failure domain** is a set of components that can fail together because they share a dependency. Typical nesting, from small to large: process, host, rack (power and top-of-rack switch), availability zone (independent power, cooling and network within a region), region, and provider. Larger domains fail more rarely but with larger impact; a design chooses the largest domain whose loss it will tolerate automatically, and documents the rest as accepted risk. Most services target zone-level tolerance by default and add region-level tolerance only when the SLO or the business impact justifies the cost and complexity of multi-region data replication (see the chapters on replication and on multi-region designs).

blocks.text:
In **active-passive** (hot standby) one node serves and a standby replicates its state; a detector promotes the standby on failure. It is simple and suits systems with one writer (a relational primary). Its costs are idle capacity, a detection-and-promotion delay (seconds to minutes) and the risk that asynchronous replication loses recently acknowledged writes (the databases material covers synchronous and asynchronous replication and the RPO consequence). In **active-active** all nodes serve traffic simultaneously; a failure removes a node from the balancer's pool, which is fast and needs no promotion. It requires that the survivors hold spare capacity and that shared data be safe to write from several places: stateless tiers are trivially active-active, while multi-writer databases need conflict resolution.

Two further properties decide whether failover works. Detection must be reliable and fast (a health check interval and failure threshold of 5 s x 3 gives 15 s), and false positives must be rare because an unnecessary failover is itself an outage. The standby path must be exercised regularly: an untested failover is a hypothesis, not a capability. A risk specific to failover is split brain, where two nodes both believe themselves primary; the fencing and leader-election techniques that prevent it belong to the chapter on consistency and coordination.

#### Graceful degradation

When a dependency fails or load exceeds capacity, a service can return a reduced result instead of an error: serve cached or stale data, hide the recommendations panel, accept writes into a queue and confirm later, or fall back to a default. Degradation must be designed: each feature is classified as essential (checkout payment) or optional (recommendations), optional features are isolated behind timeouts and breakers, and the degraded behaviour is tested. The benefit is that partial failure of an optional component does not consume the availability budget of the essential function.

#### Timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency

These techniques are implemented in Spring with Resilience4j and covered in the Spring microservices resilience material; the design-level rules are summarised here.

- **Timeouts**: every remote call has a timeout, derived from the downstream p99 plus a margin and bounded by the caller's own deadline. A call without a timeout can hold a thread indefinitely. Timeouts must decrease along the call chain (the client waits 2 s, the gateway 1.5 s, the service 1 s), otherwise a caller abandons a request while downstream work continues, wasting capacity. Propagating a deadline with the request removes the guesswork.
- **Retries** convert transient failures into successes, but only for idempotent operations and only with exponential backoff and random jitter, a limited number of attempts, and a retry budget (for example, retries may add at most 10 percent to the request volume). Unbounded or synchronised retries cause the retry storm demonstrated below.
- **Circuit breakers** stop calling a dependency that is failing so that callers fail fast and the dependency can recover.

blocks.text:
- **Idempotency** makes a repeated request equivalent to a single one. Reads and PUT-style replacements are naturally idempotent; creating an order or charging a card is not, and needs an idempotency key: the client generates a unique key per logical operation, the server stores the key with the result, and a repeated request returns the stored result instead of repeating the side effect. Idempotency is what makes retries, queue redelivery and client re-submission safe.

#### Backpressure and load shedding

When offered load exceeds capacity, the work that cannot be served must be refused somewhere. **Backpressure** pushes the signal upstream so that producers slow down: a bounded queue that blocks or rejects, a credit-based protocol, HTTP 429 or 503 with a Retry-After header, TCP flow control. **Load shedding** deliberately drops excess work, preferably the least valuable first (batch before interactive, anonymous before authenticated, retries before first attempts), so that the work that is accepted completes within its deadline.

blocks.text:
Queue bounds follow from Little's law. A service that completes 1 000 requests per second and whose clients time out after 1 second can usefully hold at most about 1 000 requests in its queue: a request admitted behind more than 1 000 others waits longer than the client will, and is served after the client has given up, which is wasted work that also delays later requests. An unbounded queue therefore converts overload into universal timeout, while a bounded queue with rejection preserves the throughput of the accepted share.

#### Retry storms and cascading failures

A **retry storm** occurs when failures trigger retries, retries add load, and the added load causes more failures. With layered retries the amplification multiplies: if three layers each make up to three attempts, one user request can produce 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 calls to the innermost dependency while it is failing, precisely when it is least able to serve them.

A **cascading failure** is a failure that spreads: the loss of a node shifts its load onto the survivors, which become overloaded and fail in turn.

blocks.text:
The arithmetic is simple. With N nodes at utilisation u, the loss of one node raises the utilisation of the survivors to u x N / (N - 1). Three nodes at 70 percent become 105 percent; ten nodes at 70 percent become 77.8 percent. Small clusters therefore need lower steady-state utilisation, and the margin to be maintained is that the loss of the largest failure domain must leave the survivors below saturation.

### Worked example

A request path consists of a CDN and balancer pair (99.99 percent), a gateway tier (99.99 percent), a stateless service tier of three instances in three zones (each 99.5 percent), and a relational database with a primary and a synchronous replica in different zones (99.95 percent with automated failover; assumed values). The availabilities in series are multiplied; the three instances in parallel contribute 1 - 0.005^3 = 99.99999 percent if failures were independent:

**Composite availability**

Three conclusions follow. The result, 99.93 percent, is lower than any single tier except the database, because dependencies in series accumulate. The database dominates: of 368 minutes of expected downtime, 263 minutes come from the database tier, so spending effort on a fourth service instance has no effect, while improving failover of the database does. And the 99.99999 percent of the parallel tier is an upper bound that assumes independent instances and enough capacity in two zones to carry the load; the shared deploy pipeline, the shared configuration and the shared database connection pool make the true figure lower, which is why such calculations are used to find the weakest tier and not to promise a number.

A service that depends synchronously on five other services of 99.9 percent each cannot exceed 0.999^5 = 99.5 percent unless it degrades gracefully when some of them fail; this is the quantitative argument for isolating optional dependencies.

### Hands-on: availability and retry simulations

Both programs run on JDK 21 with the single-file launcher and are one-process simulations of the stated models.

#### Series and parallel availability

The first program draws, for every simulated minute, whether each component is up (independent Bernoulli trials) and counts the minutes in which the topology works, over 60 simulated years per row. The row with a shared zone adds a common cause: a zone that is down 0.1 percent of the minutes takes both replicas with it.

blocks.title: Availability.java
Run (about 25 seconds on the build machine)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the simulated values agree with the formulas to within sampling error; ten 99.9 percent components in series lose 5 238 minutes a year (3.6 days), nearly ten times the loss of one component; two independent 99 percent replicas reach 99.99 percent; and when both replicas share a zone with 99.9 percent availability, the result is 99.89 percent, no better than the zone itself, despite the replica pair. The last row confirms the composition rule for a chain with a parallel stage.

#### Retry storm

The second program models a service of capacity 1 000 requests per second that receives 800 new requests per second (80 percent utilisation). It is fully unavailable for 5 seconds (ticks 10 to 14). Every request that is not served in its tick may be retried, up to 5 attempts in total. Three client policies are compared: immediate retry in the next second, exponential backoff with full jitter, and backoff with jitter plus a retry budget of 10 percent of the new-request rate (retries above the budget are abandoned, and those requests fail). One tick is one second and every request is treated as an independent unit.

What to notice:

- With immediate retries the offered load rises to 4 000 requests per second at the end of the outage (five times normal, four times the capacity), and the service runs at its capacity limit for 8 more seconds (ticks 15 to 22), recovering at tick 23 although the fault ended at tick 14.
- Backoff with jitter lowers the peak to 2 440 requests per second, but the retries are spread over a long period, so the offered load is still above the capacity of 1 000 at tick 29 (1 088), fifteen seconds after the outage ended, and the total number of extra requests is larger (13 864 against 11 378). Backoff alone does not bound the load; it only spreads it.
- The retry budget limits the offered load to at most 892 requests per second (1.12 times normal) and the service serves everything from tick 15. The price is that requests whose retries are refused fail permanently: the budget trades a bounded recovery for lost requests, which is acceptable only where the caller can report the failure or the work can be requeued.
- The model has no capacity-dependent collapse (served throughput stays at the capacity of 1 000 per second). Real services often lose throughput under overload through thread contention, garbage collection and timeouts, which makes the real storm worse than the simulation shows.

### Real-world problems and solutions

The scenarios below are composite illustrations of failure classes; the figures in them are illustrative and do not report a specific incident.

#### Problem 1: single point of failure

**Scenario.** A service has stateless application nodes in three zones, but all instances use one configuration service, one primary database in one zone, and a single message broker node.

**Symptoms.** Loss of the broker node halts all asynchronous processing although every application node is healthy; a zone failure containing the database primary takes the service down for 20 minutes during a manual promotion.

**Diagnosis.** A dependency diagram of the request path shows components with a single instance; the failover for the database is manual.

**Root cause.** Redundancy was applied to the visible tier only; the dependency chain contains components with availability equal to a single node and with no automated recovery.

**Fix.** Replicate each stateful component across zones (broker cluster with replication, database with synchronous replica and automated promotion, configuration with a cached last-known value in each instance so that its outage does not stop the service).

**Prevention.** For every component on the request path record the number of instances, the failure domain and the recovery action; review the list at each design change; run game days in which a component is killed.

#### Problem 2: retry storm after a brief outage

**Scenario.** A downstream service is unavailable for 30 seconds. Three layers of the caller each retry failed calls three times immediately.

**Symptoms.** After the downstream service restarts, it is overloaded again within seconds and stays unavailable for ten minutes; request volume at the downstream is five to ten times normal; callers' threads are exhausted.

**Diagnosis.** Request-rate graphs show a spike beginning when the dependency recovers; traces show multiple attempts per user request; the downstream fails with timeouts and not with business errors.

**Root cause.** Layered, immediate, unbudgeted retries multiply load (3 x 3 x 3 = 27 attempts per user request in the worst case) and synchronise clients, so the recovering service is hit by the entire backlog at once.

**Fix.** Retry in one layer only (typically the edge closest to the user); use exponential backoff with full jitter; enforce a retry budget; open a circuit breaker so that failures fail fast; let the downstream shed load with 429 and Retry-After so that callers back off.

**Prevention.** Retry policy is part of the design review; chaos tests inject a 30-second dependency outage and verify recovery without manual action.

#### Problem 3: cascading failure after the loss of one node

**Scenario.** A cluster of four nodes runs at 80 percent utilisation at peak. One node fails during the evening peak.

**Symptoms.** The three survivors rise to 107 percent, latency climbs, health checks time out, and the balancer removes a second node; the remaining two nodes receive 160 percent of capacity each and the service is down within minutes.

**Diagnosis.** Load per node shows a staircase as nodes disappear; garbage-collection pauses and queue depth grow before each failure.

**Root cause.** Capacity was planned for the healthy state: 80 percent x 4 / 3 = 107 percent after one failure. Overloaded nodes slow down, fail health checks and are ejected, which transfers still more load. **Fix.** Plan peak utilisation so that the loss of the largest failure domain leaves less than 70 to 80 percent (here: at most 60 percent with four nodes); shed load at the edge instead of queueing; limit the share of nodes that health checks may eject (a panic threshold); add autoscaling on queue depth.

**Prevention.** Capacity review for N+1 or N+2 at peak; load tests that remove a node under peak load.

#### Problem 4: failover that was never tested

**Scenario.** A database has a standby that has never been promoted in production. The primary fails.

**Symptoms.** Promotion takes 40 minutes; applications still point to the old address; the standby is found to be several minutes behind and missing a required extension.

**Diagnosis.** The runbook is out of date; connection strings are hard-coded; replication lag alarms were disabled after earlier noise.

**Root cause.** The failover path had no automation and no routine exercise, so latent faults accumulated unnoticed.

**Fix.** Automate promotion and endpoint switching (virtual address, proxy or DNS with a short TTL), monitor replication lag with an alert tied to the recovery-point objective, and keep the standby configuration identical to the primary.

**Prevention.** Perform scheduled failover drills, at least quarterly, and treat a drill failure as an incident.

#### Problem 5: no timeout on a remote call

**Scenario.** A service calls an internal API whose latency usually is 20 ms. The HTTP client has no read timeout.

**Symptoms.** When the API starts to hang (accepting connections but not responding), the caller's thread pool fills with blocked threads within a minute; the caller stops serving every endpoint, including those that do not use the API.

**Diagnosis.** A thread dump shows all worker threads waiting in socket reads; CPU is low.

**Root cause.** A missing timeout allows a single slow dependency to consume every thread of the caller (resource exhaustion by waiting).

**Fix.** Set connect and read timeouts, bound the thread or connection pool per dependency (bulkhead) so that one dependency cannot exhaust the shared pool, and add a circuit breaker.

**Prevention.** A client wrapper that makes the timeout mandatory; a lint or review rule for any outbound call.

### Questions to expect

#### 1. Define SLI, SLO and SLA and the relation between them.

An SLI is a measured quantity (for example the proportion of requests that succeed within 300 ms); an SLO is a target for that quantity (99.9 percent over 30 days); an SLA is a contract with consequences if a stated objective is missed. The SLO is set stricter than the SLA so that the team reacts before a penalty applies. The error budget is 1 minus the SLO.

1. **2. What is the availability of five services in series, each 99.9 percent, and of two replicas in**

#### parallel, each 99 percent?

Series: 0.999^5 = 99.50 percent (about 43.7 hours of downtime per year). Parallel: 1 - 0.01^2 = 99.99 percent, assuming independent failures and sufficient capacity in each replica. Shared failure causes reduce the parallel result.

#### 3. Compare active-passive and active-active.

Active-passive: one serving node, one standby; simple, no write conflicts, but idle capacity, promotion delay and possible loss of recent writes under asynchronous replication. Active-active: all nodes serve; failover is removal from rotation and is fast, but survivors need headroom and shared state needs conflict handling.

#### 4. How many nines can a design achieve with a single region?

Zone-level redundancy with automated failover commonly supports three to four nines, limited by region-wide events and by shared control planes and deployments. Higher targets require multi-region designs and disciplined change management; the target must be justified by the cost of downtime.

#### 5. Why are retries dangerous, and how are they made safe?

Retries add load during failure and, when layered or synchronised, multiply it. They are made safe by retrying only idempotent operations, using exponential backoff with jitter, limiting attempts and enforcing a retry budget, retrying in one layer, and combining retries with circuit breakers and load shedding at the callee.

#### 6. What is the difference between backpressure and load shedding?

Backpressure slows the producer (bounded queues, 429 with Retry-After, flow control) so that the system is not offered more than it can process. Load shedding discards excess work at the system boundary, choosing the least valuable first, when producers cannot or will not slow down. Both require bounded queues.

#### 7. How does a design avoid a cascading failure?

It keeps enough spare capacity to absorb the loss of the largest failure domain, bounds queues and applies admission control so that overload becomes fast rejections and not slow timeouts, uses timeouts and breakers to isolate failing dependencies, limits automatic ejection of nodes, and isolates resource pools (bulkheads) per dependency.

#### 8. What is graceful degradation?

Continuing to provide the essential function with reduced quality when a component fails: stale cache, omitted optional panel, queued writes, default values. It requires classifying features by importance in advance and testing the degraded paths.

#### 9. What is an idempotency key and when is it required?

A client-generated unique identifier for one logical operation, stored by the server with the outcome. A repeated request with the same key returns the stored outcome instead of repeating the effect. It is required for non-idempotent operations (payments, order creation) whenever retries, redelivery or double submission can occur.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- SLIs are measured, SLOs are targets, SLAs are contracts; the error budget (1 - SLO) turns reliability into a shared quantity.
- Each added nine cuts the budget tenfold and removes manual recovery: 99.9 percent allows 8.76 hours a year, 99.99 percent allows 52.6 minutes.
- Series components multiply availabilities (ten at 99.9 percent give 99.0 percent); independent parallel replicas multiply unavailabilities; shared failure domains cap the gain.
- Redundancy needs independent failure domains, spare capacity (N+1) and a failover path that is automated and tested.
- Timeouts, budgeted retries with jitter, circuit breakers and idempotency keys keep failures local; layered immediate retries multiply load (3 x 3 x 3 = 27).
- Bounded queues, backpressure and load shedding turn overload into fast rejections; with N nodes at utilisation u, losing one raises survivors to u x N / (N - 1).

The data store is the component of a design that is hardest to change after launch. Application servers are stateless and replaceable; a database holds the only copy of the business state, and its data model, consistency behaviour and failure modes constrain every other component. A design that selects a store by popularity, rather than by access pattern, typically fails in one of two ways: the workload does not fit the store (a join-heavy reporting query on a key-value system), or the store is operated at a scale it was not designed for (a single relational node taking every write).

This chapter provides a decision framework for the choice. It assumes the internals of relational and NoSQL systems (indexes, MVCC, replication, sharding, the storage engines) as covered in the databases material, and concentrates on the question a design interview poses: given these requirements, which store, and why.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Start from the access pattern, not the data shape

A store is selected by the operations that the system performs, ranked by frequency and by latency sensitivity. Four questions determine most of the decision.

1. **What are the dominant reads?** Lookup by primary key, lookup by secondary attribute, range scan, join across entities, full-text search, aggregation over many rows, or traversal of relationships.
2. **What are the dominant writes?** Single-row updates, multi-row transactions that must be atomic, append-only events, or bulk loads.
3. **What consistency is required?** Strong (every read observes the latest committed write), or eventual (a bounded or unbounded delay is acceptable). Some invariants, such as a non-negative account balance or a unique username, cannot be enforced under eventual consistency without extra machinery.
4. **What are the scale and growth?** Data volume, read and write rates, and the factor by which both are expected to grow. A workload that fits on one well-provisioned node for the next three years does not need a partitioned store.

#### Store families and their fit

rows: joins, constraints, multi-row ACID transactions, ad hoc queries with indexes
horizontal write scaling needs sharding, which removes cross-shard joins and transactions
single-key get and put at very low latency and high throughput
variable-shape records read and written as a unit, secondary indexes on fields
multi-document transactions are limited or costly, joins are manual
very high write rates, partitioned by key, tunable consistency
queries must follow the primary key design, no joins
not a system of record, eventual consistency, expensive updates
append-heavy timestamped data, compression, downsampling, retention
bulk aggregation, sharding a connected graph
scans and aggregates over billions of rows
cheap, durable storage of large immutable blobs
no queries, whole-object access, higher latency
images, video, backups, data lake files
blocks.caption: Store families, typical fit and typical limitation.

blocks.text: The families overlap in practice. A relational database with a JSON column covers many document workloads; a document database with multi-document transactions covers many relational ones. The table states default strengths, not exclusive capabilities. The decision should therefore rest on the dominant access pattern and on the operational reality of the team, not on the label of the product.

blocks.text:
#### SQL versus NoSQL: the decision in practice

The distinction is less about query language than about which guarantees the store maintains on behalf of the application. A relational store enforces schema, constraints and transactions in the database. A typical NoSQL store moves part of that responsibility into the application in exchange for horizontal scalability, flexible schema or a simpler operational model.

Relational is the default for the system of record unless a concrete requirement rules it out. The reasons: transactions remove entire classes of application bugs, ad hoc queries keep the data useful for questions that were not anticipated, and a single well-tuned node sustains thousands of writes per second and tens of thousands of indexed reads per second. A NoSQL store becomes the better choice under any of these conditions:

- The write rate or data volume exceeds what one relational primary with replicas can serve, and the access pattern is key-based, so sharding by key is natural (feed items, messages, events).
- The workload is a pure key lookup with a latency target under one millisecond (sessions, rate limiter counters).
- The record is naturally a self-contained aggregate that is read and written as one unit and has a variable shape (product pages with category-specific attributes).
- The availability requirement dictates multi-region writes with tolerance for conflicts, which leaderless and multi-leader stores support natively.

#### Row stores, column stores, OLTP and OLAP

An OLTP (online transaction processing) workload consists of many short transactions touching a few rows each; a row-oriented layout, which stores all fields of a row contiguously, serves it well because a transaction reads or writes whole rows. An OLAP (online analytical processing) workload consists of few queries scanning many rows but only a few columns; a column-oriented layout stores each column contiguously, which reads only the needed columns, compresses well (similar values adjacent) and enables vectorised execution.

Running analytical queries against the OLTP primary degrades both: long scans evict cache pages and hold resources, while the transactions that generate revenue slow down. The standard remedy is to copy data into a separate analytical store through change data capture (CDC, reading the database log) or batch export, accepting that analytics lag the source by seconds to hours.

#### Polyglot persistence and the single system of record

Polyglot persistence is the use of several store types in one system, each for the workload it serves best. The principle that keeps it manageable is a **single system of record** per entity: exactly one store holds the authoritative copy, and every other store holds a derived copy that can be rebuilt from the authoritative one or from an event log. Derived copies are updated asynchronously (CDC or events), so they are eventually consistent, and a divergence is repaired by rebuilding the copy, not by reconciling two authorities.

blocks.text:
Each additional store carries a cost: another failure domain, another backup and recovery procedure, another consistency boundary and another set of skills. A design should justify each store by a concrete access pattern that the existing stores cannot serve, and should prefer an extension of an existing store (a JSON column, a full-text index in the relational database) when the volume is moderate.

#### Specialised stores

**Search stores.** An inverted index maps each term to the list of documents containing it, which supports full-text matching and relevance ranking that a B-tree index cannot provide (see the chapter on common infrastructure components). A search store is a derived copy: documents are indexed after the system of record commits, so search results lag by a refresh interval, commonly about one second, and a rebuild path must exist.

**Object storage.** Blobs (images, video, documents) are stored as immutable objects addressed by key, with durability achieved through replication or erasure coding across failure domains. The database holds only metadata and the object key. Clients upload and download directly through signed URLs, so that application servers do not carry the bytes. Object stores offer high throughput and low cost per gigabyte but higher per-request latency than a database and no partial update of an object.

**Time-series stores.** Measurements arrive in timestamp order, are rarely updated, and are queried by time range and aggregated. The stores exploit this with append-only segments, delta and run-length compression, automatic downsampling (for example one-second data rolled up to one-minute averages after a week) and retention policies that drop old data cheaply by dropping whole partitions.

**Graph stores.** A graph store keeps edges as first-class, directly traversable structures, so a query such as friends-of-friends who like a given item costs proportional to the neighbourhood visited, not to table sizes as repeated joins would. The trade-off is that large connected graphs partition poorly, so graph stores are chosen when traversal depth matters more than horizontal write scale. Many systems that appear to need a graph store are served by two relational tables and a bounded-depth query.

### Worked example

The following selection is made for a ride-sharing style product with the assumed volumes shown. All figures are assumptions for the exercise, not measurements.

rows: create, update status, query by rider or driver; about 2,000 trips per second at peak
atomic trip and payment state, no lost update
sharded relational store; transactions keep payment and trip consistent
1,000,000 drivers, one update per 4 s = 250,000 writes per second; read latest position
low latency, loss of old pings acceptable
in-memory key-value store keyed by driver id, plus a geo index; history streamed to a log
append, query by driver and time range
time-series or wide-column store, partitioned by driver and day
search index fed by CDC from the trip store
object storage, metadata in the trip store
columnar warehouse loaded nightly and by stream
blocks.caption: Selection by workload for an assumed ride-hailing backend.

blocks.text:
The arithmetic behind the location row is the decisive one: 1,000,000 drivers divided by a 4-second update interval gives 250,000 writes per second, a rate that a single relational primary is not expected to absorb as individual transactions, whereas an in-memory key-value store partitioned by driver id handles it with a modest cluster. Trips, at 2,000 per second, are two orders of magnitude lower and carry the transactional requirement, so they stay relational.

### Hands-on

Two measurements illustrate why layout and index structure matter. The programs below run on the build machine; absolute numbers depend on the machine and on the Python interpreter overhead, so only the ratios are meaningful.

blocks.code:
import time, random, sqlite3
from array import array
random.seed(1)
N = 2_000_000
price = [random.random() * 100 for _ in range(N)]
# row layout: one tuple per row with 8 fields; column layout: one packed array per field
rows = [(i, i % 1000, price[i], i * 2, "x", 1, 2, 3) for i in range(N)]
col_price = array("d", price)
def t(fn, reps=5):
    best = 1e9
    for _ in range(reps):
        a = time.perf_counter(); r = fn(); best = min(best, time.perf_counter() - a)
    return best, r
tr, r1 = t(lambda: sum(r[2] for r in rows))
tc, r2 = t(lambda: sum(col_price))
print(f"SUM(price) over {N:,} rows, 8 fields per row")
print(f"  row layout (tuples)   : {tr*1000:7.1f} ms")
print(f"  column layout (array) : {tc*1000:7.1f} ms  ({tr/tc:.1f}x faster)")
print("  same result:", abs(r1 - r2) < 1e-3)

# point lookup with and without an index (SQLite)
con = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
con.execute("CREATE TABLE users(id INTEGER, email TEXT, name TEXT)")
con.executemany("INSERT INTO users VALUES(?,?,?)",
                ((i, f"user{i}@example.com", f"n{i}") for i in range(1_000_000)))
def q():
    sql = "SELECT name FROM users WHERE email = ?"
    return con.execute(sql, ("user987654@example.com",)).fetchone()
ts, _ = t(q, 3)
con.execute("CREATE INDEX idx_email ON users(email)")
ti, _ = t(q, 3)
print(f"Point lookup by email in 1,000,000 rows (SQLite, in memory)")
print(f"  full scan : {ts*1000:8.2f} ms")
print(f"  B-tree idx: {ti*1000:8.3f} ms  ({ts/ti:,.0f}x faster)")

blocks.text:
The first result shows the column-store advantage for aggregation: the column layout reads only the price values, contiguous in memory, while the row layout visits every tuple. The ratio in a real columnar engine is larger on disk, where reading fewer bytes dominates, and smaller when the row store already has a covering index. The second result shows that the access pattern (lookup by email) is served by a matching index and not by the store family: a relational database serves it in microseconds once the index exists. A store that lacks an index on the queried attribute degenerates to a scan regardless of its category.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: key-value store chosen, then ad hoc queries are required

**Scenario.** A team stores orders in a key-value store because the first feature is lookup by order id at high volume. Six months later support needs orders by customer, by date range and by status. **Symptoms.** Each new report requires a full scan or a new hand-maintained index table; scan jobs time out; data is duplicated in several keys that drift apart. **Diagnosis.** Query logs show scans over the full keyspace; row counts differ between the main table and the hand-built index tables. **Root cause.** The store was chosen for the first access pattern only, and the system of record cannot answer questions that were not anticipated. **Fix.** Move the system of record to a relational store (or add global secondary indexes where the store supports them), keeping the key-value store as a cache for the id lookup. Backfill from the existing data through a bulk export. **Prevention.** List the foreseeable query patterns (support, reporting, search) before choosing the system of record, and default to relational when the list is open-ended.

#### Problem 2: analytics queries on the primary database

**Scenario.** A dashboard runs a monthly aggregation over the orders table on the primary database during business hours. **Symptoms.** Checkout latency rises from 40 ms to seconds at the top of each hour; connection pool exhaustion; replication lag increases. **Diagnosis.** The slow query log shows a sequential scan lasting minutes; the buffer cache hit ratio drops during the scan. **Root cause.** A long analytical scan competes with transactions for I/O, cache pages and locks or vacuum horizons. **Fix.** Route analytics to a read replica as a first step, and then to a warehouse loaded by CDC. Apply statement timeouts to the reporting role. **Prevention.** Separate OLTP and OLAP roles and endpoints from the first release, and set per-role resource limits.

#### Problem 3: search index treated as the source of truth

**Scenario.** Product data is written directly to the search cluster, which also serves the product page. **Symptoms.** After a cluster incident, recent updates are missing; a mapping change requires reindexing and there is no authoritative copy to reindex from. **Diagnosis.** The record count in the search index differs from the count expected from order history; no other copy contains the product edits. **Root cause.** A derived-data store was used as the system of record, and it lacks the durability and transactional guarantees expected of one. **Fix.** Restore the product data from the latest snapshot and logs where possible, then introduce a relational or document system of record and a CDC pipeline that feeds the index. **Prevention.** State the system of record of every entity in the design document, and treat search, cache and warehouse as rebuildable.

#### Problem 4: too many stores for a small team

**Scenario.** A product with 20,000 users runs five database technologies chosen for individual features. **Symptoms.** Incident response is slow because few engineers know every store; backup restores were never tested for three of the five; a version upgrade is postponed for a year. **Diagnosis.** An inventory of stores shows each below 5% utilisation and several holding under 10 GB. **Root cause.** Each store was justified by a theoretical advantage at scale that the actual volume does not reach, while the operational cost is incurred immediately. **Fix.** Consolidate onto the relational database with a JSON column, a full-text index and a cache, and retire stores whose volume does not justify them. **Prevention.** Require a quantified reason (volume, rate, latency) for each additional store, and review the inventory when the workload changes.

### Questions to expect

1. **How is a database chosen in a design interview?** State the dominant access patterns, the consistency requirement and the expected scale with numbers, then map them to a store family. Name the system of record explicitly and list derived stores. Default to relational unless a quantified requirement rules it out.
2. **When is NoSQL a better choice than SQL?** When the write rate or volume exceeds a single relational primary and the access is key-based; when the latency target for key lookups is sub-millisecond; when the data is a self-contained aggregate with variable shape; or when multi-region writes are required. Otherwise the transactions and query flexibility of a relational store are valuable.
3. **Why not use one database for everything?** A single database is the correct starting point. It is split when a workload class (analytics, search, large blobs, very high write rates) harms the others or exceeds what the store can do. Splitting adds operational and consistency cost.
4. **What is polyglot persistence and what is its main risk?** Using multiple store types, each for the workload it suits. The main risk is inconsistency between copies; it is controlled with a single system of record and asynchronously derived copies that can be rebuilt.
5. **Why are columnar stores used for analytics?** Analytical queries read few columns across many rows. Column layout reads only the needed columns, compresses well and allows vectorised execution, so scans are cheaper by large factors.
6. **Why are images not stored in the database?** Large blobs inflate backups and replication, consume buffer cache and force the database to serve bytes. Object storage is cheaper and more durable for blobs, and signed URLs let clients transfer directly. The database stores the key and metadata.
7. **How is a search index kept consistent with the primary database?** By CDC or events emitted after the primary commits; the index is eventually consistent, with a lag measured in seconds, and a full reindex path from the system of record covers failures.
8. **When is a graph database justified?** When queries traverse several hops and the neighbourhood visited is small relative to the data (fraud rings, recommendations). For one or two hops, relational joins are usually sufficient.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Select a store from the dominant access patterns, the required consistency and the quantified scale, not from product reputation.
- Relational is the default system of record; leave it only for a stated, quantified reason.
- Keep exactly one system of record per entity; search, cache and warehouse are derived and rebuildable.
- Separate OLTP from OLAP early; analytical scans on the primary degrade transactions.
- Each added store adds operational cost; justify it with volume, rate or latency numbers.

A cache stores a copy of data in a faster or closer location so that repeated requests avoid the cost of the original source. In a backend system the original source is usually a database, whose latency is of the order of milliseconds and whose capacity is bounded by CPU and I/O. A cache in memory answers in well under a millisecond and absorbs the majority of reads, which converts a database-bound system into one limited by the cache tier, a tier that scales horizontally and cheaply. Caching is therefore the first optimisation applied to a read-heavy design, and the source of a large share of its subtle failures: stale data, stampedes and cold-start outages.

This chapter covers the placement of caches, the five write and read strategies, eviction, invalidation, the three classic failure modes (stampede, penetration, avalanche), HTTP and CDN caching, and sizing. The Redis material covers the data structures and the server internals; the Spring material covers the `@Cacheable` abstraction. Both are referenced, not repeated.

### Concept and mechanism

#### Why caching works

Caching is effective because request distributions are skewed: a small fraction of keys receives most of the traffic. For a Zipf distribution with exponent 1 over 100,000 keys, an LRU cache holding 20% of the keys reached an 80.6% hit ratio in the measurement later in this chapter, and a cache of 1% reached 50.6%. For uniformly distributed keys the same 20% cache reaches only about 20%. The hit ratio, and therefore the benefit, is a property of the workload, and a design must state which distribution it assumes.

With hit ratio h, cache latency L\_c and database latency L\_d, the expected latency is h x L\_c + (1 - h) x (L\_c + L\_d), since a miss pays for the cache lookup and then the database. With assumed values L\_c = 0.5 ms and L\_d = 8 ms: at h = 0.80 the mean is 0.5 + 0.2 x 8 = 2.1 ms, and at h = 0.95 it is 0.5 + 0.05 x 8 = 0.9 ms. The database load falls in the same proportion: the database receives (1 - h) of the read traffic, so moving h from 0.80 to 0.95 cuts database reads by a factor of four.

#### Where caches sit

A request can be served from several layers, each with a different scope, latency and invalidation mechanism.

blocks.text:
An in-process cache and a distributed cache are frequently combined: a small local cache with a short TTL (a few seconds) in front of the distributed cache removes the hottest keys from the network entirely, at the price of bounded staleness between instances.

#### The five access strategies

The strategies differ in who talks to the database and when a write reaches it.

simple; the cache holds only requested data; failure of the cache degrades to database reads
race between a read fill and a write (stale entry); first read after a miss is slow
the cache component loads from the database itself
application code is simpler; loading logic in one place
requires a cache that supports loaders; the same stale-fill race exists
each write goes to the cache and the database synchronously
cache is always consistent with acknowledged writes; reads after writes hit
write latency includes both; caches data that may never be read
write to the cache, acknowledge, flush to the database asynchronously, often batched
lowest write latency; coalesces repeated writes to one key
data loss if the cache node fails before the flush; the database lags
write to the database only; the cache is populated on the next read
avoids filling the cache with write-once data
a read soon after a write misses
blocks.caption: Caching strategies compared.

blocks.text: Cache-aside with delete-on-write is the default choice for most services. Write-through is used when reads of recently written data dominate and the cache is a managed component. Write-back is reserved for workloads that tolerate loss within the flush interval, such as counters and telemetry, or where the cache itself is durable and replicated.

blocks.text:
#### Eviction

When the cache is full, an eviction policy selects the entries to remove.

- **LRU** (least recently used) evicts the entry unused for the longest time. It adapts to shifting popularity and is implemented with a hash map plus a doubly linked list in O(1) per operation. A single large scan can flush the whole cache.
- **LFU** (least frequently used) evicts the entry with the fewest accesses. It protects consistently hot keys and resists scans, but an entry that was hot long ago may persist unless counts decay. Modern implementations combine frequency and recency: Caffeine uses W-TinyLFU, and Redis offers `allkeys-lfu` with a decaying counter.
- **FIFO and random** are cheap and sometimes adequate; random eviction is the baseline in the literature.
- **TTL** (time to live) is not an eviction policy for capacity but a freshness bound: an entry expires after a fixed duration whether or not the cache is full.

Redis approximates LRU by sampling a small number of keys (the `maxmemory-samples` setting) and evicting the best candidate among them, which avoids the cost of maintaining a global list. The `maxmemory-policy` setting selects the policy, for example `allkeys-lru`, `allkeys-lfu` or `volatile-ttl`.

#### TTL and jitter

A TTL bounds staleness and reclaims memory without explicit invalidation. Its value is a trade-off: a long TTL raises the hit ratio and the staleness window; a short TTL does the reverse. Entries written at the same moment with the same TTL expire at the same moment, which produces synchronised misses. Adding random jitter (for example TTL = 300 s plus a random value between 0 and 60 s) spreads the expiries.

#### Invalidation strategies

Invalidation is the hard part of caching because the cache and the database cannot be updated atomically.

1. **TTL only.** Accept staleness up to the TTL. Appropriate for data where bounded staleness is a stated requirement (a product description may lag by 5 minutes).
2. **Delete on write.** The writer updates the database, then deletes the cache entry; the next read refills it. Deleting is safer than updating the cache, because concurrent updates can then write values in the wrong order.
3. **Event-driven.** A change event (CDC from the database log, or an event published by the service) triggers invalidation in every cache, including local caches in each instance. This covers writes made by paths other than the service that owns the cache.
4. **Versioned keys.** Include a version or content hash in the key (`item:42:v17`, `app.3f9a1c.js`). New data uses a new key; old entries age out. This removes the invalidation problem for immutable content and is the standard approach for static assets.

### Worked example

The sizing below uses the 80/20 rule as a starting estimate, then replaces it with the measured curve where available. All inputs are assumptions.

blocks.text:
The design consequence is that the database is sized for 8,000 reads per second at the expected hit ratio, but must survive a short period at 40,000 per second if the cache is lost; mitigation of that case (warm-up, load shedding, request coalescing) is discussed under cold-start outages below. A cache that is required for the database to survive is an availability dependency, not an optimisation.

### Hands-on

#### An LRU cache and the effect of cache size

The program implements an LRU cache with `LinkedHashMap` in access-order mode, generates 1,000,000 requests from a Zipf distribution over 100,000 keys, and reports the hit ratio for several cache sizes.

blocks.title: LruDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java LruDemo.java
keys=100000 requests=1000000 zipf s=1.0
cache size (% of keys) | LRU hit ratio
   0.5% (   500 entries) | 44.0%
   1.0% (  1000 entries) | 50.6%
   2.0% (  2000 entries) | 57.3%
   5.0% (  5000 entries) | 66.4%
  10.0% ( 10000 entries) | 73.5%
  20.0% ( 20000 entries) | 80.6%
uniform keys, 20% cache: 19.9%
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21; the output is deterministic for the fixed seed)

blocks.text:
What to notice: the constructor argument `true` selects access order, so each `get` moves the entry to the most recent position, and `removeEldestEntry` evicts the least recently used one after an insertion. The curve rises quickly and then flattens: the first 1% of capacity yields 50.6% hits, the next 19% adds only 30 more points. The uniform case at 20% capacity gives 19.9%, which shows that the hit ratio comes from skew and not from the cache itself. This class is not thread-safe; a concurrent cache requires locking, striping or a library such as Caffeine.

#### A cache stampede and single-flight loading

The program starts 200 threads that request one expired key at the same instant, with a database load that takes 100 ms. The naive version lets every thread load the key; the single-flight version lets one thread load while the others wait for its result.

blocks.title: StampedeDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java StampedeDemo.java
200 concurrent requests for one expired key, database latency 100 ms
naive cache-aside   : database loads = 200
single-flight guard : database loads = 1
blocks.title: Run (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
What to notice: `putIfAbsent` on the in-flight map elects exactly one leader per key; the other threads block on the leader's `CompletableFuture`. The load count drops from 200 to 1. The pattern works within one process; across many application instances, each instance still issues one load, so 50 instances produce 50 loads. A distributed lock with a short lease, or the probabilistic early refresh described below, reduces that further.

### Real-world problems and solutions

#### Problem 1: cache stampede on expiry of a hot key

**Scenario.** A product page for a promoted item receives 8,000 requests per second. Its cache entry has a 10-minute TTL. **Symptoms.** Every 10 minutes the database CPU spikes to saturation for several seconds, request latency rises from 3 ms to seconds, and a share of requests fail with timeouts. **Diagnosis.** The spike period equals the TTL; the database log shows hundreds of identical queries for the same key in the same second. **Root cause.** When the entry expires, all concurrent requests miss, and each independently loads the same row. The cost of one regeneration, multiplied by the request rate during regeneration, exceeds database capacity. **Fix.** Coalesce loads per key (single flight in the instance, and a short-lease lock in the cache for cross-instance coordination). Serve the stale value while one request refreshes it (stale-while-revalidate). Use probabilistic early expiration: each reader recomputes with a probability that rises as the entry approaches expiry, so the refresh happens before the entry disappears. Add TTL jitter for populations of keys. **Prevention.** Identify hot keys by monitoring, and give them refresh-ahead loading by a background job instead of expiry on demand.

#### Problem 2: cache and database disagree after a concurrent read and write

**Scenario.** Cache-aside with delete-on-write. A reader and a writer touch the same key at the same time. **Symptoms.** A user updates a profile, receives a success response, and sees the old value for minutes until the TTL expires. The database holds the new value. **Diagnosis.** Comparing the cache entry with the row shows the older version in the cache. The timeline in the log reveals the interleaving below. **Root cause.** The reader's fill is not atomic with the database read, so a stale value can be written to the cache after the writer's delete. **Fix.** Keep a TTL as a safety net on every entry. Apply a delayed second delete (delete again 500 ms to 1 s after the write, for example through a queue), versioned writes (store the row version in the entry and refuse to overwrite a newer version with an older one), or leases (the cache issues a token on a miss and rejects a fill whose token was invalidated by a delete). For data that must not be stale, read from the database. **Prevention.** Document the staleness bound for each cached entity, and do not cache data whose invariants cannot tolerate that bound.

**Interleaving that leaves a stale entry**

blocks.code:
t1  Reader : cache miss for item:42
t2  Reader : SELECT price FROM items WHERE id = 42  -> 100 (old)
t3  Writer : UPDATE items SET price = 120 WHERE id = 42
t4  Writer : DEL item:42
t5  Reader : SET item:42 = 100            <- stale value written after the delete
t6  Later reads return 100 until the TTL expires

blocks.text:
#### Problem 3: cache penetration by requests for nonexistent keys

**Scenario.** An endpoint `GET /users/{id}` is cached by id. A crawler requests random ids that do not exist. **Symptoms.** The cache hit ratio falls from 95% to 40%, and the database receives a high rate of lookups that all return no rows. **Diagnosis.** The cache miss log shows ids outside the valid range; the database queries return empty results. **Root** **cause.** A miss for a nonexistent key is never cached, so every such request reaches the database. **Fix.** Cache the negative result with a short TTL (30 to 60 seconds). For large or unbounded key spaces, place a Bloom filter of existing ids in front of the cache and reject ids the filter reports absent (the filter never produces a false negative; see the chapter on common infrastructure components). Validate id format and range at the edge, and rate limit by client. **Prevention.** Treat the not-found case as a first-class cached outcome and monitor the ratio of misses that resolve to empty results.

#### Problem 4: cache avalanche after a restart or mass expiry

**Scenario.** A cache cluster is restarted for a version upgrade, or 100,000 keys loaded together at deployment share one TTL. **Symptoms.** Immediately after the restart (or at the common expiry instant) the database receives the full read traffic, latency rises, the connection pool is exhausted, and the service enters a failure that persists after the cache starts to fill, because slow responses cause client retries. **Diagnosis.** The cache hit ratio is near zero at the start of the incident; database QPS equals the total read QPS. **Root cause.** The database was sized for the post-cache load; with the cache empty the load exceeds capacity, and retries amplify it. **Fix.** Shed load at the service (reject or degrade a share of requests) while the cache warms; warm the cache from the top keys before routing traffic; restart cache nodes one at a time so that only a fraction of keys is cold; replicate the cache so a node failure does not lose its keys; and randomise TTLs. **Prevention.** Load test the database at the cold-cache rate, and keep a documented procedure for warm-up.

#### Problem 5: a hot key overloads one cache node

**Scenario.** A single key (a celebrity profile, a flash-sale item) receives 60% of the traffic of the cache cluster. **Symptoms.** One cache node reaches 100% CPU or network saturation while the others are idle; latency on that node rises and keys hosted by it become slow. **Diagnosis.** Per-node metrics show an imbalance; key-level sampling (for example Redis `--hotkeys` with an LFU policy, or client-side counters) identifies the key. **Root cause.** A key maps to exactly one node, so its entire load lands there, and adding nodes does not help. **Fix.** Replicate the hot key into a small in-process cache with a short TTL on every application instance, or store it under several derived keys (`item:42#0` to `item:42#7`) and read a random one. Add read replicas for the owning shard. **Prevention.** Monitor key-level skew and plan for known hot items in advance (a promotion calendar).

### HTTP caching and CDNs

HTTP caching moves the cache to the client and to intermediaries, controlled by response headers.

blocks.caption: Common caching headers.

blocks.text:
Static assets are served with a content hash in the file name and `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000,` `immutable`; a deployment changes the file name, which is the versioned-key invalidation strategy applied to HTTP. HTML and API responses use short `max-age` or `no-cache` with an ETag, so that revalidation costs one round trip and no body. A CDN adds the shared layer: `s-maxage` sets the CDN lifetime independently of the browser, and a purge API removes an object, with propagation delays that the design must tolerate. Personalised responses must carry `private` or `Vary` on the discriminating header, otherwise a shared cache may serve one user's response to another, a frequent source of data leaks.

### Questions to expect

1. **Compare cache-aside and write-through.** In cache-aside the application loads and fills on a miss and deletes on write; the cache holds only requested data and a cache outage degrades to database reads. Write-through writes to both synchronously, so the cache is consistent with acknowledged writes but write latency is higher and unread data occupies memory.
2. **Why delete the cache entry on write instead of updating it?** Two concurrent writers can update the cache in the opposite order from the database, leaving an old value indefinitely; a delete lets the next read load the current row. A delete still has a race with a concurrent read fill, so a TTL remains as a safety net.
3. **What is a cache stampede and how is it prevented?** Many concurrent misses for one expired key all load from the database. Prevent it with single-flight loading per key, stale-while-revalidate, probabilistic early refresh and TTL jitter.
4. **Distinguish penetration, stampede and avalanche.** Penetration: requests for keys that do not exist bypass the cache. Stampede: one hot key expires and many requests regenerate it. Avalanche: many keys expire or the cache is lost at once, so the database receives the full load.
5. **How is the cache size estimated?** Estimate the working set (items x entry size), choose the share to hold (80/20 as a starting point, then the measured hit-ratio curve), add headroom for overhead, and compute the database load as the miss ratio times the read rate.
6. **LRU or LFU?** LRU adapts quickly to changing popularity but is vulnerable to scans; LFU retains consistently popular keys and resists scans but adapts slowly without decay. W-TinyLFU combines both and is a strong default for local caches.
7. **How are caches kept consistent across service instances?** Local caches use short TTLs and event-driven invalidation (a broadcast or CDC event); a distributed cache gives one shared copy. State the acceptable staleness explicitly.
8. **What should not be cached?** Data whose staleness violates an invariant (account balances during a transfer, inventory at purchase time), highly personalised responses with a low reuse rate, and data that is cheap to compute.
9. **What happens when the cache goes down?** Requests fall through to the database. The design must either keep the database able to serve that load, or shed load and degrade, and must avoid the retry amplification that turns a partial outage into a full one.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- Hit ratio is a property of the key distribution; measure or state it, and size the database for the miss traffic and for the cold-cache case.
- Cache-aside with delete-on-write and a TTL is the default; the read-fill race means every entry also needs a staleness bound.
- Stampede (one hot key), penetration (absent keys) and avalanche (mass expiry or loss) have distinct fixes: single flight, negative caching with a Bloom filter, and jitter plus warm-up plus load shedding.
- Hot keys defeat sharding; replicate them locally or split them into derived keys.
- HTTP caching relies on versioned URLs for assets and validators (ETag) for dynamic responses; mark personalised responses `private`.

A single database node limits a system in three ways: it is a single point of failure, its read and write capacity is bounded, and its storage is bounded. **Replication** keeps copies of the same data on several nodes, which addresses availability and read capacity. **Partitioning** (sharding) divides the data set among nodes so that each holds a subset, which addresses write capacity and storage. Large systems use both: the data is partitioned, and each partition is replicated.

This chapter treats the placement problem as a design decision. The replication mechanics inside a particular database (the write-ahead log, logical decoding, replication slots) and the physical sharding features of particular products are covered in the databases material; the focus here is on topologies, the anomalies they introduce, the partitioning strategies, consistent hashing, and the operational problems of rebalancing and resharding.

blocks.text:
**Single leader (leader and followers).** All writes go to the leader, which appends them to a replication log; followers apply the log in order. Reads may be served by followers. Replication is **synchronous** when the leader waits for the follower to confirm before acknowledging the client, **asynchronous** when it does not, and **semi-synchronous** when it waits for at least one follower. Synchronous replication removes the loss window but couples availability and latency to the slowest awaited follower; asynchronous replication keeps the leader fast but can lose acknowledged writes if the leader fails before the followers receive them.

Failover (promoting a follower after a leader failure) has three well-known hazards. First, an asynchronous follower may lack the last acknowledged writes, which are then lost or must be reconciled. Second, if the former leader returns and still accepts writes, two leaders exist (split brain; see the chapter on consistency and coordination). Third, a timeout that is too short triggers failover on a transient pause and causes more damage than it prevents.

**Multi-leader.** Each region has a leader that accepts local writes and replicates to the other leaders asynchronously. The benefits are low write latency in every region and survival of a region failure. The cost is that two leaders can accept conflicting writes to the same record. Conflict resolution strategies are last-writer-wins by timestamp (simple, discards data and depends on synchronised clocks), application-specific merge, conflict-free replicated data types (CRDTs) for structures with a mathematically commutative merge such as counters and sets, and avoiding conflicts by routing each record to one home region.

**Leaderless.** Any replica accepts a write. A client (or a coordinator) sends the write to N replicas and considers it successful after W acknowledgements; a read contacts R replicas and returns the newest version. If W + R \> N, every read set intersects every write set (see the chapter on consistency and coordination for the quorum arithmetic). Replicas that missed a write are repaired by **read repair** (the reader writes the newest version back to stale replicas), **hinted handoff** (a node stores writes destined for an unavailable peer and delivers them later) and **anti-entropy** (background comparison of replicas, often with Merkle trees that identify differing key ranges cheaply). This is the model of the Dynamo paper and of systems derived from it.

#### Replication lag and its anomalies

With asynchronous replication a follower lags the leader by a variable delay: typically milliseconds, but seconds or more during load spikes, long transactions on the follower or network problems. A client that reads from followers can observe the following anomalies.

rows: a user writes, then reads from a follower that has not applied the write, and sees the old value
route the user's reads to the leader for a window after a write, or track the write position and read only from a follower that has reached it
successive reads hit different followers, and the second returns older data than the first
pin a user or session to one follower
causally related writes (a question and its answer) are seen out of order because they were applied on different partitions
keep causally related writes in one partition, or carry causal metadata

blocks.text:
#### Partitioning strategies

Partitioning assigns each record to one of several partitions by a **partition key**. The choice of key and of mapping function determines load balance, query cost and the ease of rebalancing.

blocks.text:
- **Range partitioning** assigns contiguous key ranges to shards. Range scans and ordered traversal are efficient, and a range can be split when it grows. The risk is skew: sequential keys (timestamps, auto-increment ids) concentrate all current writes on the shard that owns the latest range.
- **Hash partitioning** applies a hash function to the key and maps the result to a shard. The distribution is even, but adjacent keys are scattered, so range queries must contact every shard.
- **Directory-based partitioning** keeps an explicit lookup table from key (or tenant) to shard. It permits arbitrary placement, such as moving one large tenant to a dedicated shard, at the cost of a highly available lookup service.
- **Geographic partitioning** assigns data to regions for latency and data residency rules. Load follows the distribution of users and can be skewed.

The partition key should satisfy four criteria: high cardinality (many distinct values), even access frequency, inclusion in the most frequent queries (so that a query targets one shard), and stability (a key that changes forces a move between shards). User id, tenant id and order id are typical choices; country, status and boolean flags are poor ones.

#### Consistent hashing

The simple mapping `shard = hash(key) mod N` fails when N changes: nearly every key maps to a different shard, so adding one node to a cluster of N forces about N/(N+1) of the data to move and invalidates nearly all cache entries at once. **Consistent hashing** limits the movement. Both nodes and keys are hashed onto the same circular space (for example 0 to 2^64 - 1). A key belongs to the first node found moving clockwise from the key's position. Adding a node takes over the arc preceding its position from one neighbour; removing a node hands its arc to the next node. On average only 1/N of the keys move when a node is added to a cluster of N - 1 nodes.

With one position per physical node, arcs have very unequal lengths and load is unbalanced. The standard remedy is **virtual nodes**: each physical node is hashed to many positions (tens to hundreds), so that it owns many small arcs, the load averages out, and a joining node takes small arcs from every existing node, which spreads the transfer work across the cluster. Heterogeneous nodes receive a number of virtual nodes proportional to their capacity.

**Lookup rule**

blocks.text:
Related schemes serve the same purpose. **Rendezvous (highest random weight) hashing** scores every node for each key and selects the highest score; it needs no ring state and balances well, but the lookup costs O(N). **Fixed** **logical partitions** (used, for example, by Redis Cluster with 16,384 hash slots, and by Kafka partitions and Elasticsearch shards) hash keys to a fixed, large number of partitions and keep a table assigning partitions to nodes; rebalancing moves whole partitions, and the key-to-partition mapping never changes.

#### Rebalancing

Rebalancing moves data when nodes are added, removed or overloaded. Three approaches are common.

1. **Fixed number of partitions.** Create many more partitions than nodes (for example 1,024 partitions on 8 nodes). A new node steals whole partitions from existing nodes. The partition count must be chosen in advance, since it limits the maximum cluster size and the minimum partition size.
2. **Dynamic splitting.** Partitions split when they exceed a size threshold and merge when they shrink, as in range-partitioned stores. The number of partitions adapts to data volume, at the cost of more complex metadata.
3. **Proportional to nodes.** A fixed number of partitions per node, with new nodes splitting existing partitions randomly (the virtual node approach).

Rebalancing is expensive: it moves data across the network, competes with foreground traffic, and may run while a node is already overloaded. Automatic rebalancing triggered by a transient failure can aggravate the failure. Many systems therefore require operator confirmation, or throttle the transfer rate.

#### Cross-shard operations

When the data is partitioned, queries and transactions that span partitions become expensive.

- **Queries without the partition key** use scatter-gather: the request goes to every shard and the results are merged. Latency is that of the slowest shard, so the tail latency of the query is worse than that of any shard, and capacity does not scale with shard count because every query consumes work on every shard.
- **Secondary indexes** are either **local** (each shard indexes its own data; a query by the indexed attribute is scattered) or **global** (a separate index partitioned by the indexed attribute; a query contacts one index partition, but writes update an index on another shard, usually asynchronously).
- **Joins** across shards are avoided by denormalising (embedding the needed attributes), by co-locating related tables on the same partition key (all rows of a customer on one shard), or by broadcasting a small table to every shard.
- **Transactions** across shards require two-phase commit or a saga (see the chapter on consistency and coordination), both of which cost latency and availability. The better design chooses the partition key so that a business transaction stays within one shard.

#### Resharding without downtime

Changing the partitioning scheme or the number of shards while serving traffic follows a fixed sequence: copy, verify, cut over, clean up.

blocks.text:
The router holds a versioned shard map, so the cutover is an atomic change of one record. Reads move first or together with writes, depending on whether the new shard has verified as complete. Rollback is possible until the old shard is decommissioned, which is why the cleanup is delayed.

### Worked example

The shard count for an assumed order store is derived from capacity limits and growth, then rounded to a power of two of logical partitions.

blocks.caption: Shard sizing for an assumed order store.

blocks.text:
The result shows the purpose of fixed logical partitions: the application sees 64 partitions from the first day, and growth to 18 or 32 nodes is a matter of moving whole partitions, not of changing the key mapping. Each node is also replicated (assumed one leader and two followers per partition group), so the physical node count is three times the shard count in a fully replicated deployment; that figure belongs in the cost estimate.

### Hands-on

#### Consistent hashing with virtual nodes

The program places 10 nodes on a ring with a varying number of virtual nodes per node, assigns 100,000 keys, and reports the load balance. It then adds an 11th node and counts the keys that change owner, with and without consistent hashing.

10 nodes, 100000 keys, ideal load per node = 10000
vnodes/node | min    max    max/ideal | stddev/mean

adding an 11th node to 10 nodes:
ring, 100 vnodes: 9074 keys move (9.1%); ideal 1/11 = 9.1%

What to notice: with one position per node the most loaded node holds 3.38 times the ideal share and one node holds 66 keys; with 100 virtual nodes the spread falls to a standard deviation of 9.1% of the mean, and with 500 to 6.2%, with diminishing returns as the number of virtual nodes grows. When the 11th node joins, the ring moves 9,074 keys, matching the ideal 1/11 = 9.1%, while `hash mod N` moves 90.7%. `TreeMap.ceilingEntry` is the clockwise lookup; the wrap-around to the first entry closes the ring.

#### Hot shards, rebalancing and read-your-writes

The two programs below are single-process simulations: they model the distribution of keys and replication delays; they do not measure a real database.

blocks.title: shard.py

blocks.code:
$ python3 shard.py

hash  sharding, 20,000 sequential inserts -> writes per shard [5048, 4964, 4945, 5043]
hash mod N, 4 -> 5 shards: 159942 of 200000 keys move (80.0%)

blocks.title: Run (Python 3, deterministic seeds)

blocks.text: What to notice: with range partitioning, the 20,000 newest sequential inserts all land on the last shard, while hash partitioning spreads them within about 1% of equal. Moving from 4 to 5 shards with `mod N` relocates 80% of keys (the general value is N/(N+1) for adding one shard, here 4/5); fixed logical partitions relocate 19.9%, close to the ideal 1/5. A hot key defeats hash partitioning: the shard owning it receives 62,118 of 100,000 reads; splitting the key into eight sub-keys reduces the maximum to 31,343.

blocks.title: repl.py

blocks.code:
$ python3 repl.py
random follower                      stale reads of own write: 36 of 40
leader for 500 ms after own write    stale reads of own write:  0 of 40
